docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Argo CD Terraform Controller runs Terraform and OpenTofu from Argo CD, GitOps style, with plan approval, drift detection and a UI extension. It is an add-on: no changes to Argo CD are required.

A Terraform object (infra.argocd.io/v1alpha1) describes a Git or OCI source, variables, backend, approval mode and outputs. Argo CD syncs the object like any other manifest; the controller fetches the source, plans, waits for approval when asked to, applies, detects drift and writes outputs. Argo CD shows the result through its normal health model, resource actions and a Terraform entry in the sidebar.

flowchart TB
    subgraph argocd[Argo CD]
        app[Application]
        ui[UI extension<br/>health · actions]
    end

    tf[Terraform<br/>infra.argocd.io/v1alpha1]
    ctrl[Controller<br/>fetch source · plan · approve · apply · drift]
    runner[Runner Pod<br/>tofu or terraform]

    subgraph out[Results]
        state[(State Secret)]
        plan[Plan Secret<br/>+ readable ConfigMap]
        outputs[Outputs Secret]
    end

    cloud[(Cloud / provider<br/>resources)]

    app -- sync --> tf
    ui -. read / approve .-> tf
    tf --> ctrl
    ctrl -- gRPC + mTLS --> runner
    runner --> state
    runner --> plan
    runner --> outputs
    runner --> cloud

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Terraform object describing a Git or OCI source, variables, backend, approval mode, outputs and health checks. Argo CD syncs the object; the controller does the rest.
  • Terraform and OpenTofu in one runner image; choose per object with spec.runner.binary: auto | terraform | tofu.
  • Plan / approve / apply with manual approval by plan ID (from Git, kubectl or the Argo CD UI), auto approval, plan-only and drift-detection-only modes.
  • Drift detection on every interval, with automatic remediation in auto mode.
  • State in a Kubernetes Secret through Terraform's kubernetes backend by default, or any other backend (s3, gcs, azurerm, …) and Terraform Cloud.
  • Outputs to a Secret, health checks, dependsOn between stacks, destroy on deletion (optionally deleting the state too), state force-unlock.
  • Argo CD integration through supported extension points only: health assessment and resource actions in argocd-cm, and a UI extension adding a Terraform sidebar dashboard — every Terraform object across your Applications, with a graph of what each one manages (Kubernetes or not: VPCs, buckets, databases…), plan output and an approve button — plus a resource tab, an Application details tab and an application view.
  • Isolation: the controller holds source credentials and talks to a per-object runner Pod over mTLS; the runner only executes the binary with its own ServiceAccount.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• New here? Follow the Getting started walkthrough: it installs everything on a cluster that already runs Argo CD and takes a sample through plan, approval and apply.
  • Running it for a team? The Operator Manual covers installation and upgrades, the Argo CD integration, state backends and the Terraform/OpenTofu runner.
  • Writing Terraform objects? The User Guide explains the approval workflow, sources, variables and credentials, drift detection, outputs, dependencies and destroy semantics, with complete examples and the full specification reference.
  • Something off? Troubleshooting and the FAQ.
  • Contributing? See the Developer Guide.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Alpha. The API group infra.argocd.io/v1alpha1 may change before v1. Releases, images and Helm charts are published from the GitHub repository.

docs.title: How is this different from the Flux tofu-controller?
docs.text: It is deliberately similar — same runner-Pod model, same state and approval concepts — but built for Argo CD: the Terraform object is a plain manifest an Application syncs, health and actions come from argocd-cm, and the UI is an Argo CD extension. There is no dependency on Flux's source controller; the object carries its own spec.source. See Architecture.

docs.title: How is it different from Crossplane, or from a provider's Kubernetes operator?
docs.text: Those model each cloud resource as a Kubernetes object with their own providers. This controller runs your existing Terraform/OpenTofu code unchanged — modules, providers, state and all — and gives Argo CD a single object per stack to approve, apply and watch. Use whichever matches how your team already works; they can coexist.

docs.title: Does it change Argo CD?
docs.text: No. It installs a CRD and a controller, adds two keys to argocd-cm (health and actions Lua) and an init container to argocd-server that downloads the UI extension. Everything uses Argo CD's documented extension points; see Argo CD integration.

docs.title: Terraform or OpenTofu?
docs.text: Both are in the runner image; choose per object with spec.runner.binary. auto prefers OpenTofu. See Terraform vs OpenTofu.

docs.title: Is it production-ready?
docs.text: It is alpha: the API (infra.argocd.io/v1alpha1) may still change, and it has had limited exposure. The controller is designed conservatively (manual approval by default, infrastructure kept on deletion by default, hardened Pods), so the blast radius of a bug is small, but evaluate it on non-critical stacks first.

docs.title: Why does Argo CD show my Application as Suspended?
docs.text: A plan is waiting for approval. That is the default (approvePlan: "") and it intentionally blocks later sync waves. Approve it in the UI, with kubectl, or by committing the plan ID — or use approvePlan: auto. See Plan approval.

docs.title: I approved in the UI and the plan went back to pending.
docs.text: Argo CD with selfHeal reverted spec.approvePlan to the value in Git. Either approve from Git or add the ignoreDifferences described in Argo CD integration › GitOps considerations.

docs.title: Where is my state?
docs.text: By default in Secret tfstate-<workspace>-<name> in the object's namespace, via Terraform's kubernetes backend (status.stateSecretName). Any other backend works through spec.backendConfig. See State.

docs.title: Can I adopt infrastructure that already has a state file?
docs.text: Yes. Either point spec.backendConfig.customConfiguration at the existing backend, or import the state into the Kubernetes backend once (restore procedure in State › Backup and restore), or run terraform import from a laptop against the Secret (State › Working with the state from the CLI).

docs.title: What happens when I delete the object?
docs.text: Plan and outputs objects are removed; the infrastructure and the state are kept unless spec.destroyResourcesOnDeletion: true (and spec.tfstate.deleteOnDestroy: true for the state). See Destroy and deletion.

docs.title: Why is the object Degraded with DriftDetected?
docs.text: Something changed the infrastructure outside Terraform. In manual mode the controller reports and waits; press Re-plan and approve to reconcile it, or use approvePlan: auto to let it self-heal. See Drift detection.

docs.title: How do I pass variables and credentials?
docs.text: spec.vars/varsFrom/values/tfVarsFiles for variables; envFrom, fileMappings or workload identity on the runner ServiceAccount for credentials. See Variables and credentials.

docs.title: How do I see output values?
docs.text: Names are in status.availableOutputs; values are only in the Secret named by spec.writeOutputsToSecret (kubectl get secret … -o go-template=…). The UI never shows values. See Outputs.

docs.title: Can two objects share one state or one set of resources?
docs.text: Don't. One state per object; use dependsOn and outputs to connect stacks. Two objects on the same state would fight over the lock and each other's resources.

docs.title: Can I run the same configuration for several environments?
docs.text: Yes — several objects with the same source and path but different vars, workspace or backendConfig.secretSuffix. Each gets its own state Secret (tfstate-<workspace>-<suffix>).

docs.title: How big can my repository be?
docs.text: The source is archived and sent to the runner in one gRPC message, bounded by --runner-grpc-max-message-size (4 MiB default). Use spec.source.git.ignore to exclude what the stack does not need, or raise the limit. See Controller configuration.

docs.title: The Terraform sidebar entry / tab is missing.
docs.text: The extension is not installed or the browser cached the old extensions.js. kubectl -n argocd exec deploy/argocd-server -- ls /tmp/extensions/resources/ should list extension-terraform.js; then hard-refresh. See Troubleshooting › Nothing in the Argo CD UI.

docs.title: The dashboard does not show an object I created with kubectl.
docs.text: The dashboard aggregates through the Argo CD Applications API, so it lists Terraform objects that belong to Applications you are allowed to see. Objects applied outside Argo CD are not shown (they still work).

docs.title: Why are plan outputs visible to anyone who can see the Application?
docs.text: The readable plan is stored in a ConfigMap so Argo CD can display it (Argo CD redacts Secret data). If plans may contain sensitive values, set spec.storeReadablePlan: none. See Security.

docs.title: Where do I report bugs or ask for features?
docs.text: GitHub issues. Security issues: please use a private security advisory.

docs.title: How do I contribute?
docs.text: See the Developer Guide: the repository builds with make, tests run with envtest and kind, and the UI builds in a container.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
Everything below is copy-and-paste-able and only needs helm and kubectl pointed at a cluster that already runs Argo CD in the argocd namespace. Set the two variables first.

export VERSION=v0.0.7          # release of the Argo CD Terraform Controller
export TF_NAMESPACE=team-a     # namespace that will host Terraform objects

docs.title: 1. Install everything with Helm
docs.text:
One command installs the controller, creates the runner identity in ${TF_NAMESPACE}, and integrates with the Argo CD running in argocd (health assessment, resource actions and the UI extension):

helm install argocd-terraform-controller \
  oci://quay.io/redhatworkshops/argocd-terraform-controller-helmchart --version ${VERSION#v} \
  --namespace argocd-terraform-controller-system --create-namespace \
  --set runner.namespaces="{${TF_NAMESPACE}}" \
  --wait

The chart checks that Argo CD is present before doing anything and fails with instructions otherwise (Argo CD in another namespace: --set argocd.namespace=<ns>). A Helm hook patches argocd-cm and argocd-server, detecting the server container name automatically, and waits for argocd-server to roll out. helm uninstall reverts those patches. Every piece is a knob — see Installation.

docs.title: 2. Let the runner manage cluster resources (walkthrough only)
docs.text:
The sample used below manages a Namespace and a ConfigMap with the Kubernetes provider, so for this walkthrough let tf-runner do that. Use a narrower ClusterRole in real deployments; cloud providers instead get credentials through spec.runner.podTemplate.spec.env / envFrom, workload identity or spec.fileMappings — see Using cloud credentials.

kubectl create clusterrolebinding tf-runner-${TF_NAMESPACE}-sample \
  --clusterrole=cluster-admin --serviceaccount=${TF_NAMESPACE}:tf-runner

docs.title: 3. Verify
docs.text:
kubectl -n argocd-terraform-controller-system get deploy
kubectl -n ${TF_NAMESPACE} get serviceaccount tf-runner
kubectl -n argocd get configmap argocd-cm -o jsonpath='{.data}' | grep -o 'infra.argocd.io_Terraform' | sort -u
kubectl -n argocd exec deploy/argocd-server -- ls /tmp/extensions/resources/
# extension-terraform.js

Argo CD loads extensions at startup and browsers cache them; hard-refresh the UI (Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+R) once argocd-server has rolled out.

Without Helm (plain manifests) The same three pieces, applied by hand from the release assets: 
# Controller: CRD, RBAC, Deployment
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/redhat-developer/argocd-terraform-controller/releases/download/${VERSION}/install.yaml
kubectl -n argocd-terraform-controller-system rollout status deploy/argocd-terraform-controller-controller-manager

# Runner identity in the Terraform namespace (repeat per namespace)
kubectl create namespace ${TF_NAMESPACE} --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
kubectl apply -n ${TF_NAMESPACE} -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: tf-runner
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: tf-runner
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: argocd-terraform-controller-runner-role
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: tf-runner
EOF

# Argo CD: health + actions
kubectl patch configmap argocd-cm -n argocd --type merge \
  --patch "$(curl -fsSL https://github.com/redhat-developer/argocd-terraform-controller/releases/download/${VERSION}/argocd-cm-patch.yaml)"

# Argo CD: UI extension. The server container is "argocd-server" (upstream
# install.yaml) or "server" (Argo CD Helm chart); detect it and match it.
SERVER_CONTAINER=$(kubectl get deploy argocd-server -n argocd -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].name}')
curl -fsSL https://github.com/redhat-developer/argocd-terraform-controller/releases/download/${VERSION}/argocd-server-extension-patch.yaml \
  | sed "s/- name: argocd-server/- name: ${SERVER_CONTAINER}/" \
  | kubectl patch deployment argocd-server -n argocd --patch-file /dev/stdin
kubectl -n argocd rollout status deploy/argocd-server

# Optional: let the controller reuse Argo CD repository credentials
kubectl apply -n argocd -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/redhat-developer/argocd-terraform-controller/${VERSION}/config/argocd/argocd_repo_reader_binding.yaml

docs.title: 4. Create an Application that syncs a Terraform object
docs.text:
The UI extension renders inside Applications, so sync the Terraform object through Argo CD rather than applying it directly. This Application syncs the sample from this repository:

kubectl apply -n argocd -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: terraform-sample
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/redhat-developer/argocd-terraform-controller
    targetRevision: ${VERSION}
    path: config/samples
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: ${TF_NAMESPACE}
  syncPolicy:
    automated: {}
EOF

The sample (config/samples/infra_v1alpha1_terraform.yaml) fetches examples/kube-namespace from Git, runs it with approvePlan: auto, writes the outputs to the Secret terraform-sample-outputs and destroys the resources when the object is deleted.

Watch it progress:

kubectl get terraform -n ${TF_NAMESPACE} -w

After a couple of minutes (provider download included):

kubectl get terraform terraform-sample -n ${TF_NAMESPACE} -o jsonpath='{.status.binary}{"\n"}{.status.lastAppliedRevision}{"\n"}'
kubectl get secret -n ${TF_NAMESPACE} tfstate-default-terraform-sample terraform-sample-outputs
kubectl get namespace terraform-demo
kubectl get configmap tfplan-default-terraform-sample-readable -n ${TF_NAMESPACE} -o jsonpath='{.data.tfplan}'

In the Argo CD UI click Terraform in the left sidebar: the dashboard lists team-a/terraform-sample with its state; click it for the graph (Git source → Terraform → the state/plan/outputs objects → the kubernetes_namespace and kubernetes_config_map resources it manages, with their IDs), the plan output, outputs, conditions and events. Inside the terraform-sample Application the Terraform node also has a Terraform tab, and the view switcher gains a Terraform view.

docs.title: Try manual approval
docs.text:
kubectl patch terraform terraform-sample -n ${TF_NAMESPACE} --type merge \
  -p '{"spec":{"approvePlan":"","vars":[{"name":"namespace","value":"terraform-demo-2"}]}}'

The next plan has changes and waits: the object is Suspended in Argo CD with the plan ID in its message. Approve it with the Approve plan button in the Terraform tab, or:

PLAN=$(kubectl get terraform terraform-sample -n ${TF_NAMESPACE} -o jsonpath='{.status.plan.pending}')
kubectl patch terraform terraform-sample -n ${TF_NAMESPACE} --type merge -p "{\"spec\":{\"approvePlan\":\"${PLAN}\"}}"

(The Application shows the patched object as OutOfSync; with automated.selfHeal Argo CD would revert it — see the GitOps considerations in Argo CD integration.)

docs.title: 5. Clean up
docs.text:
kubectl delete application terraform-sample -n argocd --cascade=foreground   # prunes the Terraform object, which destroys terraform-demo
kubectl delete clusterrolebinding tf-runner-${TF_NAMESPACE}-sample
helm uninstall argocd-terraform-controller -n argocd-terraform-controller-system   # also reverts the Argo CD patches

Delete the Application first and wait for it to disappear: the destroy runs through the controller's finalizer, so the controller must still be installed when the Terraform object goes away. The ${TF_NAMESPACE} namespace is kept (helm.sh/resource-policy: keep); remove it yourself if it was only for this walkthrough.

docs.title: Using cloud credentials
docs.text: The sample above only needs Kubernetes access, so the runner's ServiceAccount is enough. Real stacks need provider credentials delivered to the runner Pod: a credentials file through spec.fileMappings, environment variables through spec.runner.podTemplate.spec.envFrom, or workload identity on the tf-runner ServiceAccount. All three, with copy-and-paste examples, are in Variables and credentials.

docs.title: What happens on each reconciliation
docs.text:
1. The source is resolved (git ls-remote / registry HEAD) and fetched when the revision changed; the tree is archived and shipped to the runner.
  2. A runner Pod <name>-tf-runner is created (or reused) in the object's namespace and connected over mTLS.
  3. The backend configuration, variables and files are generated; init and workspace selection run.
  4. If nothing changed since the last apply, a refresh-only plan detects drift.
  5. Otherwise a plan is produced and stored in a Secret (plus a readable copy in a ConfigMap). With manual approval the object waits here.
  6. The approved plan is applied, outputs are written, health checks run.
  7. The runner Pod is deleted (spec.runner.alwaysCleanup) and the object is requeued after spec.interval.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
api/v1alpha1/          CRD types, status helpers; api/planid plan ID derivation
cmd/manager            controller binary        cmd/runner   runner binary
internal/controller    reconciliation (setup, plan, apply, drift, outputs, finalizer)
internal/runner        gRPC server executing terraform/tofu (runner.proto)
internal/mtls          CA + per-namespace runner certificates
internal/source        git / OCI fetchers, Argo CD credential lookup
internal/plan          plan <-> Secret/ConfigMap encoding (gzip, chunking)
internal/tarball       source archiving / safe extraction
internal/argocd        tests for config/argocd/lua
config/                kustomize: crd, rbac, manager, runner (per-namespace), argocd (component), samples
charts/                Helm chart (CRD synced from config/crd)
ui/extension           Argo CD UI extension (TypeScript, built in a Node container)
hack/argocd-cm         renders config/argocd/lua into argocd-cm-patch.yaml
test/e2e               kind end-to-end tests

docs.title: Everyday commands
docs.text:
make generate manifests     # deepcopy, CRD, RBAC, gRPC code, argocd-cm patch
make test                   # unit + envtest (needs terraform or tofu in PATH)
make lint                   # golangci-lint
make build                  # bin/manager, bin/runner (never `go build ./cmd/...` at the root: a stray binary there breaks the runner's 4 MiB source limit; CI runs make verify-tree-size)
make docker-build docker-build-runner
make test-e2e               # kind: builds images, deploys, applies with tofu and terraform
make ui-test ui-build build-extension   # UI, in a node:22 container
make helm-sync helm-lint verify-argocd-overlay   # helm-sync copies CRDs + the argocd-cm Lua patch into the chart
make build-docs serve-docs   # documentation site, in a python:3.12 container

The envtest suite starts the controller with INSECURE_LOCAL_RUNNER=1 and an in-process runner on localhost, using the local tofu/terraform binary and a local backend stored outside the working directory. The e2e suite serves the local checkout from a git daemon Pod inside kind unless E2E_SOURCE_URL (with E2E_SOURCE_REF, E2E_SOURCE_PATH) points elsewhere.

docs.title: Running locally against a cluster
docs.text:
make install                                 # CRD
INSECURE_LOCAL_RUNNER=1 go run ./cmd/runner --grpc-port 30000 &   # no TLS, local binary
INSECURE_LOCAL_RUNNER=1 DISABLE_TF_K8S_BACKEND=1 go run ./cmd/manager --runner-grpc-port 30000

INSECURE_LOCAL_RUNNER=1 makes the controller dial localhost instead of creating runner Pods (it still issues the mTLS secret with a localhost SAN when the runner is started with --tls-secret-name).

docs.title: Changing the gRPC protocol
docs.text: Edit internal/runner/runner.proto, run make proto (buf + protoc-gen-go, installed into bin/), implement the server method in internal/runner and the client call in internal/controller.

docs.title: Changing the Argo CD customizations
docs.text: Edit config/argocd/lua/** and run make argocd-cm (also part of make manifests) to regenerate config/argocd/argocd-cm-patch.yaml. Tests in internal/argocd exercise the scripts with gopher-lua. The UI mirrors the health logic in ui/extension/src/model.ts; keep them in sync.

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text:
Bump export VERSION=vX.Y.Z in docs/getting-started.md so the guide stays copy-pasteable (make verify-release-version TAG=vX.Y.Z checks it; the Release workflow fails early if it does not match the tag), then tag vX.Y.Z. CI pushes the quay.io/redhatworkshops/argocd-terraform-controller-{manager,runner} images, publishes the Helm chart to oci://quay.io/redhatworkshops/argocd-terraform-controller-helmchart (tag X.Y.Z), builds the UI extension tarball, the install manifest, the Argo CD patches and the chart tarball, and attaches them to the GitHub release.

The chart is named argocd-terraform-controller-helmchart so Helm's OCI push lands it in its own Quay repository; nameOverride in values.yaml keeps the rendered resources named argocd-terraform-controller. The Quay robot (QUAY_USERNAME / QUAY_PASSWORD) needs write access to that repository, as it does for the image repositories.

docs.title: Documentation site
docs.text:
The docs are MkDocs with the Material theme, configured like the Argo CD docs: mkdocs.yml at the repository root, sources under docs/, Python requirements in docs/requirements.txt. Nothing needs to be installed on the host:

make serve-docs             # live reload on http://localhost:8000
make build-docs             # strict build into site/ (what CI runs)

strict: true turns broken links, missing nav entries and unknown relative links into build failures. Links from docs to files in the repository (code, manifests) must be absolute GitHub URLs; links between pages are relative .md paths. GitHub-style callouts (> [!NOTE]) render on both GitHub and the site through the gh-admonitions plugin.

The Docs workflow (.github/workflows/docs.yml) runs only when docs/**, mkdocs.yml or .readthedocs.yaml change: pull requests get a strict build; pushes to main also deploy to the gh-pages branch, served at https://redhat-developer.github.io/argocd-terraform-controller/. The other workflows ignore documentation changes.

The configuration is Read the Docs-ready (.readthedocs.yaml, like argoproj/argo-cd). To move the site there: import the repository on readthedocs.org, which picks up .readthedocs.yaml and sets READTHEDOCS_CANONICAL_URL (used by site_url in mkdocs.yml), then remove the deploy job from docs.yml and delete the gh-pages branch.

docs.title: Operator Manual
docs.text:
This section is for the people who install and run the controller and wire it into Argo CD.

  • Architecture — components, what happens on each reconciliation, the status model and the isolation boundaries.
  • Installation and upgrades — install with a manifest, Helm or Kustomize, create the runner identity per namespace, upgrade release by release knowing which piece changed, uninstall safely.
  • Controller configuration — every flag and environment variable, Helm value mapping, sizing and availability.
  • Argo CD integration — health assessment, resource actions, the UI extension, reusing Argo CD repository credentials and RBAC for users.
  • State backends, backup and restore — the default Kubernetes backend, other backends and Terraform Cloud, locks, backup and restore, working with the state from the CLI.
  • Terraform vs OpenTofu — choosing the binary, mixing them, custom runner images.
  • Security — trust boundaries, hardening, tenancy, RBAC for people, secrets, supply chain.
  • Metrics — scraping the controller, useful metrics and alerts.
  • Troubleshooting — by Ready reason and by symptom.

For a first end-to-end run on a test cluster, use Getting started instead; it is the copy-and-paste version of this manual.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
The controller turns a Terraform object into Terraform or OpenTofu runs executed in a short-lived runner Pod, and reports the result back through the object's status so that Argo CD can display it like any other resource.

flowchart LR
    subgraph argocd[Argo CD namespace]
        app[Application]
        srv[argocd-server<br/>UI extension]
        cm[argocd-cm<br/>health + actions Lua]
    end

    subgraph sys[argocd-terraform-controller-system]
        mgr[Controller manager]
    end

    subgraph ns[Terraform object's namespace]
        tf[Terraform]
        runner[Runner Pod<br/>name-tf-runner]
        state[(tfstate Secret<br/>+ lock Lease)]
        plan[(tfplan Secret<br/>+ readable ConfigMap)]
        outputs[(outputs Secret)]
        tls[(runner TLS Secret)]
    end

    src[(Git / OCI source)]
    cloud[(Providers:<br/>AWS, GCP, Kubernetes, …)]

    app -- sync --> tf
    srv -. Argo CD API .-> app
    cm -. health, actions .-> tf
    mgr -- watch / status --> tf
    mgr -- fetch --> src
    mgr -- create --> runner
    mgr -- gRPC over mTLS :30000 --> runner
    mgr --> tls
    runner --> state
    runner --> plan
    runner --> outputs
    runner --> cloud

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
Component Runs where Role Controller manager (cmd/manager) Deployment in argocd-terraform-controller-system, one leader Watches Terraform objects; resolves and fetches sources; creates runner Pods; drives them over gRPC; writes status, conditions and events; owns the mTLS CA Runner (cmd/runner) One Pod per Terraform object, in the object's namespace, only for the duration of a run Receives the source archive, generates backend/variables files, executes terraform/tofu through terraform-exec, stores plans and outputs as Secrets/ConfigMaps using its own ServiceAccount (tf-runner) Argo CD customizations (config/argocd) argocd-cm and an init container on argocd-server Health assessment, resource actions (approve, re-plan, suspend, resume, force-unlock) and the UI extension; see Argo CD integration

Only the controller has credentials to read sources; only the runner has permissions in the object's namespace. The two meet over a per-namespace mutual-TLS gRPC connection.

docs.title: A reconciliation, step by step
docs.text:
1. Trigger. The object was created or changed (a new metadata.generation), spec.interval elapsed, the infra.argocd.io/reconcile annotation was set, or a previous run asked for a retry. Status-only updates do not trigger runs.
  2. Dependencies. If spec.dependsOn is set, every dependency must be Ready at its current generation (and, for the same source, at the same revision); otherwise the object is Progressing/DependencyNotReady and is retried. A finalizer is added to each dependency so it cannot be deleted first.
  3. Source. The controller resolves the revision (git ls-remote, or the OCI manifest digest). If it changed since the last run, the tree is fetched, filtered by ignore, and archived. Argo CD repository credentials can be reused (Sources).
  4. Runner. A Pod <name>-tf-runner is created in the object's namespace from spec.runner (image, ServiceAccount, podTemplate) with a mounted server certificate issued by the controller's CA. The controller waits for it to become ready (--runner-creation-timeout) and dials it by Pod IP.
  5. Setup. The archive is uploaded; the runner writes backend_override.tf (the Kubernetes backend by default, see State), generated.auto.tfvars.json from spec.vars/varsFrom/values, any spec.fileMappings, and the .tfrc from cliConfigSecretRef; then runs init (with -upgrade and -force-copy) and selects the workspace.
  6. Drift detection. When nothing changed since the last apply, a refresh-only plan checks the real infrastructure against the state. No drift → done (Ready/NoDrift). Drift → DriftDetected; in auto mode the run continues to re-plan and apply, otherwise it stops and reports. See Drift detection.
  7. Plan. plan -out produces a binary plan stored in Secret tfplan-<workspace>-<name> and a human-readable copy in ConfigMap tfplan-<workspace>-<name>-readable. The plan ID (plan-<ref>-<sha>) goes to status.plan.pending. Without approval the run stops here; Argo CD shows Suspended. See Plan approval.
  8. Apply. With approvePlan: auto, spec.force, or a matching plan ID the controller re-plans once more (to make sure the approved plan is still current) and applies. Failures set Ready=False with a TFExec* reason and schedule a retry.
  9. Outputs, inventory, health checks. Outputs are written to spec.writeOutputsToSecret, the list of managed resources is recorded in status.inventory, and spec.healthChecks run against the outputs. See Outputs and Dependencies and health checks.
  10. Cleanup. The working directory is removed, the runner Pod is deleted (spec.runner.alwaysCleanup, default) and the object is requeued after spec.interval.

Deletion follows the same path through a finalizer: with spec.destroyResourcesOnDeletion a destroy plan is applied first; plan and output objects are removed; the state Secret is kept unless spec.tfstate.deleteOnDestroy is set. See Destroy and deletion.

docs.title: Status model
docs.text:
The object carries standard metav1.Conditions. Ready is the one Argo CD's health check reads:

Ready Reason (examples) Meaning Argo CD health True TerraformAppliedSucceed, NoDrift, TerraformOutputsWritten, HealthChecksSucceeded, TerraformPlannedNoChanges Last run succeeded and the infrastructure matches Healthy Unknown Progressing, TerraformPlannedWithChanges, DependencyNotReady Working, or waiting for a human Progressing, or Suspended when a plan awaits approval False TFExecPlanFailed, TFExecApplyFailed, SourceFetchFailed, LockHeld, DriftDetected, HealthChecksFailed, RetryLimitReached, AccessDenied Something needs attention Degraded any Suspended spec.suspend: true Suspended

Additional conditions (Plan, Apply, Output, HealthCheck, StateLocked, Reconciling, Stalled) record the last result of each phase. Events with the same reasons are emitted on the object; the Argo CD UI shows them under the Terraform tab and in the dashboard. The full list is in the specification reference.

docs.title: Isolation model
docs.text:
• Credentials split. Source credentials (Git/OCI, including Argo CD's) are read by the controller and never reach the runner; the runner receives a tarball. Provider credentials given through env/envFrom or workload identity reach the runner only; fileMappings content is read by the controller and forwarded over the mTLS channel (Variables and credentials). The controller itself never holds a cloud identity or runs the binary.
  • Per-namespace runners. A runner runs as the tf-runner ServiceAccount of the object's namespace with a Role limited to Secrets, ConfigMaps and Leases there. Different teams' namespaces get different identities, and cloud permissions can be bound per namespace (or per object with spec.runner.serviceAccountName).
  • mTLS. The controller runs a CA (rotated, --ca-validity-duration) and issues a server certificate per namespace (terraform-runner.tls Secret). The runner only accepts the controller's client certificate; nothing else can instruct it.
  • Hardened Pods. Manager and runner run as non-root with a read-only root filesystem, all capabilities dropped and a RuntimeDefault seccomp profile. The runner's /tmp and /home/runner are emptyDirs that die with the Pod.
  • No Argo CD privileges. The UI extension uses the logged-in user's Argo CD session and RBAC; the controller only needs read access to Argo CD's repository Secrets, and only if that feature is enabled.

See Security for the operator's checklist.

docs.title: Repository map
docs.text:
For contributors, the code follows the component split above:

Path Contents api/v1alpha1 Terraform types, condition helpers, naming helpers (StateSecretName, RunnerPodName) internal/controller Reconciler: setup, drift, plan, apply, outputs, finalizer, runner Pod management internal/runner gRPC server executed inside the runner image (runner.proto) internal/mtls CA and certificate rotation internal/source Git and OCI fetchers, Argo CD credential lookup internal/plan, internal/tarball Plan Secret chunking, source archives config/ Kustomize: CRD, RBAC, manager, runner identity, Argo CD component, samples charts/ Helm chart ui/extension Argo CD UI extension (TypeScript/React)

More in the Developer Guide.

docs.title: Argo CD integration
docs.text: Everything here is configuration of a stock Argo CD; no Argo CD code or image changes are involved. The pieces live in config/argocd and are packaged as a Kustomize Component.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
With the Helm chart (default) nothing needs doing: a post-install hook merges the health/actions Lua into argocd-cm and adds the UI extension init container to argocd-server, detecting the server container name; a pre-delete hook reverts both. Every step is a value under argocd.integration.* — see Installation › Helm.

Without the chart, or with argocd.integration.enabled=false, pick one of the following.

As a component of your Argo CD kustomization:

# kustomization.yaml
namespace: argocd
resources:
- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-cd/stable/manifests/install.yaml
components:
- https://github.com/redhat-developer/argocd-terraform-controller/config/argocd?ref=main

Or patch an existing installation:

kubectl patch configmap argocd-cm -n argocd --type merge --patch-file config/argocd/argocd-cm-patch.yaml
# The argocd-server container is named "argocd-server" (upstream install.yaml)
# or "server" (Helm chart); detect it so the strategic merge matches.
SERVER_CONTAINER=$(kubectl get deploy argocd-server -n argocd -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].name}')
sed "s/- name: argocd-server/- name: ${SERVER_CONTAINER}/" config/argocd/argocd-server-extension-patch.yaml \
  | kubectl patch deployment argocd-server -n argocd --patch-file /dev/stdin
kubectl apply -n argocd -f config/argocd/argocd_repo_reader_binding.yaml

If the container name does not match, strategic merge appends a container with no image and the API rejects the patch with spec.template.spec.containers[0].image: Required value.

With the Argo CD Helm chart, the native way is to copy the two resource.customizations.* keys of argocd-cm-patch.yaml into configs.cm and the init container / volume of the server patch into server.initContainers, server.volumeMounts, server.volumes (the chart already names the container server, so no rename is needed there).

docs.title: Health assessment
docs.text:
config/argocd/lua/health.lua maps a Terraform object to an Argo CD health:

Health When Healthy Ready=True — applied, no drift, outputs written (or plan-only with a plan) Progressing no status yet, initialising, planning, applying, dependency not ready Suspended spec.suspend, or a plan is waiting for manual approval Degraded the last run failed, drift detected, state locked, stalled

Suspended holds up later sync waves, so an Application can create a database with Terraform in wave 0 and deploy the workload that needs it in wave 1; the deployment waits for the approval and the apply.

docs.title: Resource actions
docs.text:
config/argocd/lua/actions defines actions available from the resource menu, the Argo CD CLI (argocd app actions run) and the UI extension buttons:

Action Effect approve-plan spec.approvePlan = status.plan.pending replan sets the infra.argocd.io/reconcile annotation; the controller reconciles immediately and discards an unapproved pending plan suspend / resume toggles spec.suspend force-unlock spec.tfstate.forceUnlock = auto (only enabled while status.lock.pending is set)

docs.title: GitOps considerations
docs.text:
Actions mutate the live object. If the Application has automated sync with selfHeal, Argo CD reverts the change on the next sync — which is often the intended "approvals must come from git" policy. To allow approving from the UI while keeping the object in git, ignore those fields:

spec:
  ignoreDifferences:
  - group: infra.argocd.io
    kind: Terraform
    jsonPointers:
    - /spec/approvePlan
    - /spec/suspend
    - /spec/tfstate/forceUnlock
    - /metadata/annotations/infra.argocd.io~1reconcile
  syncPolicy:
    syncOptions:
    - RespectIgnoreDifferences=true

Approving from git is simply committing spec.approvePlan: <plan id>; the ID is in the Ready condition message, the TerraformPlanSucceed event and the UI.

docs.title: UI extension
docs.text:
The extension (ui/extension) registers three things:

  • a Terraform entry in the sidebar (system-level extension at /extensions/terraform): a dashboard of every Terraform object across all Applications you can see — counts by state, search and filters, and a detail page per object with a graph from the source, through the Terraform object and its Kubernetes objects (state, plan, outputs, runner), to every resource the state manages — including non-Kubernetes resources such as VPCs, buckets or databases, grouped by provider and type with their IDs (from status.inventory, recorded after each apply when spec.enableInventory is true, the default). Plan output, outputs, conditions, recent events and the action buttons are on the same page.
  • a Terraform tab on infra.argocd.io/Terraform resources inside an Application;
  • a Terraform tab in the Application details panel (next to Summary, Parameters, Manifest and Events) and a Terraform application view in the toolbar, both listing the Terraform objects of one Application.

Everything is read through the Argo CD API (/api/v1/applications, …/{app}/resource, …/{app}/resource-tree, …/{app}/events) and actions run through POST …/{app}/resource/actions; all of it is authorised by Argo CD RBAC (applications, get and applications, action/infra.argocd.io/Terraform/<action>). No backend service and no proxy extension are needed. Consequently the dashboard shows Terraform objects that are managed by an Argo CD Application; objects applied outside of Argo CD are not listed.

The human readable plan is stored in a ConfigMap (spec.storeReadablePlan: human, the default) because Argo CD redacts Secret data in its API. The ConfigMap is owned by the Terraform object and therefore appears in the Application tree.

The extension is installed by the argocd-extension-installer init container in argocd-server-extension-patch.yaml, downloading argocd-terraform-extension.tar.gz from a GitHub release. The application view appears when the Application's resources include a Terraform object or when the Application has the label infra.argocd.io/has-terraform: "true"; the details panel tab is always present (Argo CD has no per-Application filter for resource tabs) and says so when the Application manages no Terraform objects.

docs.title: Reusing Argo CD repository credentials
docs.text:
Set spec.source.git.useArgoCDRepoCredentials: true to let the controller look up the credentials Argo CD already has for the URL (Secrets labelled argocd.argoproj.io/secret-type: repository or repo-creds, plus argocd-ssh-known-hosts-cm for SSH). This requires:

  • the controller flag --argocd-namespace (set from ARGOCD_NAMESPACE), and
  • read access to Secrets/ConfigMaps in that namespace (config/argocd/argocd_repo_reader_binding.yaml, or argocd.repoCredentials.enabled in the Helm chart).

docs.title: RBAC for users
docs.text:
Argo CD users approve plans through the resource action, so grant it in the Argo CD RBAC policy:

p, role:platform, applications, action/infra.argocd.io/Terraform/approve-plan, */*, allow
p, role:platform, applications, action/infra.argocd.io/Terraform/replan, */*, allow

docs.title: Terraform vs OpenTofu
docs.text:
The runner image ships both CLIs:

Binary Version build arg Source tofu TOFU_VERSION ghcr.io/opentofu/opentofu:<version>-minimal terraform TERRAFORM_VERSION releases.hashicorp.com (checksum verified)

Select per object:

spec:
  runner:
    binary: auto        # default: tofu if present in the image, otherwise terraform
    # binary: terraform
    # binary: tofu

status.binary records what actually ran, e.g. tofu 1.13.1.

Both binaries are driven through terraform-exec with identical commands (init -upgrade -force-copy, plan -out, show, apply, output, force-unlock), so every feature of the controller works the same with either. Variables, backend and .tfrc handling are also identical; the only difference users see is the version line in status.binary and the plan text.

docs.title: Mixing binaries
docs.text: Different Terraform objects can use different binaries, including objects that depend on each other. The state format is compatible between current Terraform and OpenTofu releases, but switching an existing object from one to the other is a one-way migration in practice (newer OpenTofu state versions may not be readable by Terraform). Pin binary explicitly for production stacks.

docs.title: Custom runner images
docs.text:
Use spec.runner.image or the controller's RUNNER_POD_IMAGE to point at a derived image, e.g. with extra tooling or a single binary:

FROM quay.io/redhatworkshops/argocd-terraform-controller-runner:latest
USER root
RUN rm /usr/local/bin/terraform && apk add --no-cache aws-cli
USER 65532:65532

Build the stock image with other versions:

make docker-build-runner RUNNER_IMG=my/runner:dev TERRAFORM_VERSION=1.9.8 TOFU_VERSION=1.8.5

Licensing: Terraform is distributed under the BUSL-1.1; OpenTofu under the MPL-2.0. Pick the binary that fits your usage; auto prefers OpenTofu.

docs.title: Controller configuration
docs.text: The controller manager is configured with command-line flags (and a few environment variables) on its Deployment. With the manifest install, edit the Deployment argocd-terraform-controller-controller-manager in argocd-terraform-controller-system; with Helm, set the values in the right column.

docs.title: Flags
docs.text:
Flag Default Helm value Purpose --concurrent 4 controller.concurrent Terraform objects reconciled in parallel. Each active reconcile holds one runner Pod; raise it for many small stacks, lower it to cap cluster load. --runner-image $RUNNER_POD_IMAGE runner.image.repository / tag Default runner image; overridable per object with spec.runner.image. --runner-grpc-port 30000 runner.grpcPort Port the runner's gRPC server listens on inside the Pod. --runner-grpc-max-message-size 4 (MiB) runner.grpcMaxMessageSize Upper bound for one gRPC message, which bounds the size of the source archive shipped to the runner. Raise it for large repositories or use spec.source.git.ignore. --runner-creation-timeout 2m runner.creationTimeout How long to wait for a runner Pod to become Ready (image pull, scheduling). --runner-rpc-timeout 30m runner.rpcTimeout Timeout for the setup phase (upload, init, provider downloads). Plans and applies are not bounded by it. --cluster-domain cluster.local controller.clusterDomain DNS domain used in the runner certificate's SANs. --no-cross-namespace-refs true controller.noCrossNamespaceRefs Deny spec.dependsOn and spec.cliConfigSecretRef pointing at other namespaces (AccessDenied). Set to false for a single-tenant cluster that needs cross-namespace dependencies. --argocd-namespace $ARGOCD_NAMESPACE argocd.namespace Namespace of Argo CD; enables spec.source.git.useArgoCDRepoCredentials. Empty disables the feature. --ca-validity-duration 168h mtls.caValidityDuration Lifetime of the runner mTLS CA. --cert-rotation-check-frequency 30m mtls.rotationCheckFrequency How often the CA is checked for rotation. --cert-lookahead-interval 1h mtls.lookaheadInterval Rotate the CA this long before it expires. --leader-elect false (manifest sets it) controller.leaderElection Required when running more than one replica. --metrics-bind-address 0 (disabled; manifest sets :8443) — Metrics endpoint; see Metrics. --metrics-secure true — Serve metrics over HTTPS with authn/authz. --health-probe-bind-address :8081 — Liveness/readiness probes. --zap-log-level, --zap-encoder, … info, console controller.logLevel, controller.extraArgs Logging (controller-runtime zap flags). Use --zap-log-level=debug while troubleshooting.

Anything not covered by a value can be passed with controller.extraArgs / controller.extraEnv in the chart.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text: Variable Purpose RUNNER_POD_IMAGE Default for --runner-image. The release install.yaml pins it to the release's runner image. ARGOCD_NAMESPACE Default for --argocd-namespace. RUNTIME_NAMESPACE The controller's own namespace (set from the Pod's metadata.namespace); used to garbage-collect stale runner TLS Secrets at startup. DISABLE_TF_K8S_BACKEND=1 Use backend "local" instead of the Kubernetes backend when the object sets neither backendConfig nor cloud. Tests only — state is lost with the runner Pod. INSECURE_LOCAL_RUNNER=1 Talk to an in-process runner without mTLS. Tests only.

docs.title: Sizing and availability
docs.text:
• Replicas. The manager is a standard leader-elected controller: run 2 replicas for fast failover; only the leader reconciles. Runner Pods are not affected by a manager restart — a run in progress is retried from the start by the new leader (plans are idempotent; applies resume from the state).
  • Concurrency. Memory use is dominated by source archives held during upload; CPU by Git fetches. The chart defaults (100m/128Mi requests, 1/1Gi limits) comfortably handle the default --concurrent=4.
  • Runner resources. Terraform's own CPU/memory needs vary wildly with the provider. Set spec.runner.podTemplate.spec.resources per object or namespace defaults with a LimitRange; see Runner.
  • Quotas. If a namespace ResourceQuota prevents creating the runner Pod, the object reports RunnerQuotaExhausted and retries after spec.retryInterval.

docs.title: Namespaces and tenancy
docs.text: The controller watches Terraform objects cluster-wide. What limits a team is the runner identity in its namespace (which Secrets/Leases it may write, which cloud role it maps to) and --no-cross-namespace-refs. Three ClusterRoles for users ship with the install — terraform-viewer-role, terraform-editor-role, terraform-admin-role — to bind per namespace or cluster-wide. See Security.

docs.title: Installation and upgrades
docs.text:
Every release publishes the same set of assets on the GitHub releases page. Pick a version once and use it for all of them:

export VERSION=v0.0.6
export RELEASE=https://github.com/redhat-developer/argocd-terraform-controller/releases/download/${VERSION}
Asset What it installs Lives in install.yaml Terraform CRD, controller RBAC, the controller Deployment (manager and runner images pinned to the release) namespace argocd-terraform-controller-system argocd-terraform-controller-helmchart-<ver>.tgz Helm chart equivalent of install.yaml, plus the runner identity for runner.namespaces. Also published as an OCI chart at oci://quay.io/redhatworkshops/argocd-terraform-controller-helmchart (tag <ver>) wherever you install it argocd-cm-patch.yaml Health assessment and resource actions (Lua) for infra.argocd.io/Terraform ConfigMap argocd-cm argocd-server-extension-patch.yaml Init container that downloads the UI extension into argocd-server Deployment argocd-server argocd-terraform-extension.tar.gz, checksums.txt The UI extension bundle; fetched by the init container above, not applied by hand —

The Helm chart installs all of it — controller, runner identity and the Argo CD integration — and is the recommended path. The other assets exist for people who prefer plain manifests or need to apply the pieces separately.

docs.title: Helm (recommended)
docs.text:
helm install argocd-terraform-controller \
  oci://quay.io/redhatworkshops/argocd-terraform-controller-helmchart --version ${VERSION#v} \
  --namespace argocd-terraform-controller-system --create-namespace \
  --set runner.namespaces="{team-a,team-b}" \
  --wait

What happens:

  1. Preflight. At render time the chart looks up the Argo CD namespace (argocd.namespace, default argocd). If it is missing the install fails before touching anything, with the three ways out printed in the error (--set argocd.namespace=…, --set argocd.integration.required=false, or disable the integration). helm template and helm lint are unaffected — the check only runs against a live cluster.
  2. Controller. CRD, RBAC, Deployment in the release namespace.
  3. Runner identity. For every namespace in runner.namespaces (plus the release namespace): the namespace itself if missing (runner.createNamespaces, kept on uninstall), the tf-runner ServiceAccount and its RoleBinding. runner.namespaces is deliberately not defaulted — you decide where Terraform may run.
  4. Argo CD integration (post-install/post-upgrade hook Job, because argocd-cm and argocd-server belong to Argo CD and cannot be rendered by this chart): verifies the ConfigMap and Deployment exist, merges the health/actions Lua into argocd-cm, adds the argocd-extension-installer init container to argocd-server — detecting the server container name, argocd-server or server — and waits for the rollout.
  5. Repository credentials. A Role in the Argo CD namespace that lets the controller reuse Argo CD's repository Secrets (spec.source.git.useArgoCDRepoCredentials).

helm uninstall runs the same hook in reverse (argocd.integration.cleanupOnUninstall): the Lua keys and the init container are removed and Argo CD is back to how it was.

docs.title: Knobs
docs.text:
Everything has a default that works with a stock Argo CD in argocd; override only what differs in your environment.

Value Default Purpose runner.namespaces [] Required in practice. Namespaces that may host Terraform objects runner.createNamespaces true Create missing runner namespaces (annotated helm.sh/resource-policy: keep) runner.extraClusterRoles [] Extra ClusterRoles to bind to every tf-runner (e.g. for the Kubernetes provider) argocd.namespace argocd Where Argo CD lives argocd.integration.enabled true Do the Argo CD integration at all argocd.integration.required true Fail when Argo CD is not found; false installs the controller alone and warns argocd.integration.cleanupOnUninstall true Revert the patches on helm uninstall argocd.integration.customizations.enabled / .configMapName true / argocd-cm Health + actions Lua argocd.integration.uiExtension.enabled / .deploymentName true / argocd-server UI extension argocd.integration.uiExtension.containerName "" (auto) Server container to mount into; auto-detects the first container argocd.integration.uiExtension.version chart appVersion Release to download the extension from argocd.integration.uiExtension.extensionURL / .checksumURL derived Full URL overrides for mirrors / air-gapped clusters argocd.integration.uiExtension.installer.image pinned argocd-extension-installer The init container image argocd.integration.uiExtension.installer.waitForRollout / .rolloutTimeout true / 5m Wait for argocd-server after patching argocd.integration.hook.image pinned alpine/k8s Image of the hook Job (needs sh, kubectl, jq) argocd.integration.hook.* sane backoffLimit, activeDeadlineSeconds, ttlSecondsAfterFinished, resources, nodeSelector, tolerations, podAnnotations argocd.repoCredentials.enabled true Role to read Argo CD repository Secrets controller.* see values.yaml concurrent, replicas, logLevel, extraArgs, resources, scheduling … (Controller configuration) image.tag, runner.image.tag chart appVersion Pin images independently metrics.* enabled, HTTPS Metrics Service and optional ServiceMonitor (Metrics)

Using the Argo CD Helm chart and preferring to keep the integration in its values? Set argocd.integration.enabled=false and copy the two resource.customizations.* keys from the release's argocd-cm-patch.yaml into configs.cm, and the init container / volume from argocd-server-extension-patch.yaml into server.initContainers, server.volumeMounts, server.volumes.

The chart tarball attached to each release (argocd-terraform-controller-helmchart-<ver>.tgz) is the same chart for air-gapped installs — mirror it and the hook image first.

docs.title: Without Helm
docs.text: The same pieces, applied by hand.

docs.title: 1. Controller
docs.text:
From the release manifest:

kubectl apply -f ${RELEASE}/install.yaml
kubectl -n argocd-terraform-controller-system rollout status deploy/argocd-terraform-controller-controller-manager

The Deployment carries two environment variables you may want to change: RUNNER_POD_IMAGE (the runner image containing terraform and tofu) and ARGOCD_NAMESPACE (defaults to argocd; used to reuse Argo CD repository credentials).

Or with Kustomize:

kubectl apply -k "https://github.com/redhat-developer/argocd-terraform-controller/config/default?ref=${VERSION}"

The kustomize base in Git references the latest image tags; pin them in your overlay (images: for the manager, the RUNNER_POD_IMAGE env for the runner) or use install.yaml, which the release pipeline already pins.

docs.title: 2. Runner identity per namespace
docs.text:
Runner Pods run as the tf-runner ServiceAccount of the Terraform object's namespace and write Secrets, ConfigMaps and Leases there (state, plans, outputs, locks). Create it in every namespace that hosts Terraform objects (the Helm chart does this for runner.namespaces):

kustomize build "https://github.com/redhat-developer/argocd-terraform-controller/config/runner?ref=${VERSION}" \
  | kubectl apply -n team-a -f -

This binds tf-runner to the argocd-terraform-controller-runner-role ClusterRole, which only grants what the runner itself needs. Permissions for what the Terraform configuration manages are separate:

  • Kubernetes provider → bind additional (Cluster)Roles to tf-runner, or use runner.extraClusterRoles in the chart.
  • Cloud providers → see Variables and credentials.

docs.title: 3. Argo CD
docs.text:
Configuration only; nothing in Argo CD is rebuilt. Details and the RBAC for users are in Argo CD integration.

kubectl patch configmap argocd-cm -n argocd --type merge \
  --patch "$(curl -fsSL ${RELEASE}/argocd-cm-patch.yaml)"

# The server-extension patch mounts the extension into the argocd-server
# container. Its name depends on the install method (upstream install.yaml:
# "argocd-server"; Helm chart: "server"), so detect it and rewrite the patch.
SERVER_CONTAINER=$(kubectl get deploy argocd-server -n argocd -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].name}')
curl -fsSL ${RELEASE}/argocd-server-extension-patch.yaml \
  | sed "s/- name: argocd-server/- name: ${SERVER_CONTAINER}/" > /tmp/argocd-terraform-server-patch.yaml
kubectl patch deployment argocd-server -n argocd --patch-file /tmp/argocd-terraform-server-patch.yaml
kubectl -n argocd rollout status deploy/argocd-server

# Optional: let the controller reuse Argo CD repository credentials
kubectl apply -n argocd -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/redhat-developer/argocd-terraform-controller/${VERSION}/config/argocd/argocd_repo_reader_binding.yaml

Verify the extension landed, then hard-refresh the browser (Argo CD caches extensions.js):

kubectl -n argocd exec deploy/argocd-server -- ls /tmp/extensions/resources/
# extension-terraform.js

Note

The server-extension patch merges into the server container by name. The upstream install.yaml names it argocd-server; the Argo CD Helm chart names it server. If the name does not match, strategic merge appends a container with no image and the API rejects the patch with spec.template.spec.containers[0].image: Required value. The SERVER_CONTAINER detection above handles both.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
With Helm, one command upgrades everything and the hook re-applies the Argo CD integration (re-pinning the UI extension to the new release and rolling argocd-server):

helm upgrade argocd-terraform-controller \
  oci://quay.io/redhatworkshops/argocd-terraform-controller-helmchart --version ${VERSION#v} \
  --namespace argocd-terraform-controller-system --reuse-values --wait

Hard-refresh the Argo CD UI afterwards (browsers cache extensions.js). Rolling update; Terraform objects and state are untouched. CRD updates are additive within v1alpha1.

Without Helm, releases are independent per component; read the release notes and apply only the assets that changed:

Changed in the release Run Controller, CRD, RBAC, runner (Go code, API types) kubectl apply -f ${RELEASE}/install.yaml Health or actions (config/argocd/lua) The argocd-cm patch above. Argo CD reloads it live — no restart. UI extension (ui/extension) The argocd-server patch above. Re-applying it re-pins the download URL to the new release and triggers a rollout; a plain rollout restart would re-download the old bundle.

docs.title: Uninstalling
docs.text:
Delete the Terraform objects (or the Argo CD Applications that own them) first and wait for them to go: destroys run through the controller's finalizer, so the controller must still be present. State Secrets are kept unless spec.tfstate.deleteOnDestroy was set; see State.

helm uninstall argocd-terraform-controller -n argocd-terraform-controller-system

The pre-delete hook removes the Lua keys from argocd-cm and the init container from argocd-server (unless argocd.integration.cleanupOnUninstall=false). Runner namespaces created by the chart are kept; delete them yourself. The CRD is kept too (Helm never deletes CRDs) — kubectl delete crd terraforms.infra.argocd.io removes it and every remaining Terraform object with it.

Without Helm: kubectl delete -f ${RELEASE}/install.yaml, then revert the Argo CD patches by hand if wanted (remove the resource.customizations.*.infra.argocd.io_Terraform keys from argocd-cm and the extension-terraform init container, extensions volume and mount from argocd-server). They are inert without the CRD.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text: The controller exposes Prometheus metrics from the controller-runtime metrics server. With the manifest install the endpoint is enabled on :8443 (HTTPS) behind a Service argocd-terraform-controller-controller-manager-metrics-service in argocd-terraform-controller-system; scraping requires a token with get on the /metrics non-resource URL (the install ships a metrics-reader ClusterRole for that).

docs.title: Scraping
docs.text:
With the Prometheus Operator, apply the ServiceMonitor from the repository's config/prometheus (it targets the https port and uses the Prometheus ServiceAccount token):

kubectl apply -k "https://github.com/redhat-developer/argocd-terraform-controller/config/prometheus?ref=${VERSION}"
kubectl create clusterrolebinding argocd-terraform-metrics-reader \
  --clusterrole=argocd-terraform-controller-metrics-reader \
  --serviceaccount=monitoring:prometheus-k8s

The shipped ServiceMonitor uses insecureSkipVerify: true for the self-signed serving certificate. For production, mount a certificate from cert-manager into the manager (--metrics-cert-path) and set serverName/ca in the tlsConfig instead — the commented monitor_tls_patch.yaml in the same directory shows the fields.

The install also contains a NetworkPolicy that admits traffic to the metrics port only from namespaces labelled metrics: enabled:

kubectl label namespace monitoring metrics=enabled

To scrape over plain HTTP in a test cluster, pass --metrics-bind-address=:8080 --metrics-secure=false to the manager.

docs.title: What is exported
docs.text:
Everything controller-runtime provides, labelled with controller="terraform" where applicable:

Metric Use it for controller_runtime_reconcile_total{result=…} Reconcile rate; result="error" for failing runs controller_runtime_reconcile_errors_total Errors over time controller_runtime_reconcile_time_seconds (histogram) How long runs take — Terraform plan/apply duration dominates controller_runtime_max_concurrent_reconciles Confirms --concurrent controller_runtime_active_workers How many objects are being reconciled right now (each holds a runner Pod) workqueue_depth{name="terraform"} Backlog: objects waiting for a worker workqueue_queue_duration_seconds How long objects wait before a worker picks them up rest_client_requests_total API server traffic leader_election_master_status 1 on the active replica go_*, process_* Runtime health

A useful starting alert set:

- alert: TerraformReconcileErrors
  expr: rate(controller_runtime_reconcile_errors_total{controller="terraform"}[15m]) > 0
  for: 30m
- alert: TerraformBacklog
  expr: workqueue_depth{name="terraform"} > 10
  for: 15m
- alert: TerraformControllerDown
  expr: absent(up{job=~".*argocd-terraform-controller.*"} == 1)
  for: 5m

docs.title: Per-object status instead of metrics
docs.text:
There are no per-Terraform-object metrics yet (drift count, pending approvals, last apply age). That information is in the object's status and in Argo CD:

  • pending approvals: kubectl get tf -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.status.plan.pending != "") | .metadata.name', or the counters at the top of the Terraform dashboard in Argo CD;
  • drift: Ready condition reason DriftDetected, Argo CD health Degraded, and a Warning event with the drift plan;
  • staleness: status.lastSuccessfulReconcileAt, status.lastDriftDetectedAt.

Argo CD's own argocd_app_info{health_status=…} metric therefore reflects Terraform objects too: an Application that contains a Terraform object waiting for approval reports health_status="Suspended", a failing one Degraded. Alerting on Argo CD health is often the simplest way to cover Terraform runs.

Per-object metrics are a reasonable future addition; please open an issue with the labels you would need.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: Terraform can create anything its credentials allow, and its state contains every attribute of every resource it manages. This page lists what the controller does to contain that, and what is left for you to decide.

docs.title: Trust boundaries
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    user[Argo CD user] -- RBAC: applications get / action --> argocd[Argo CD]
    argocd -- sync, actions --> tf[Terraform object]
    ctrl[Controller] -- watches --> tf
    ctrl -- reads --> gitcreds[(Git/OCI credentials<br/>Argo CD repo Secrets)]
    ctrl -- mTLS gRPC --> runner[Runner Pod<br/>SA tf-runner]
    runner -- reads --> cloudcreds[(Provider credentials<br/>Secrets / workload identity)]
    runner -- writes --> state[(State, plan, outputs<br/>Secrets in the namespace)]
    runner --> cloud[(Cloud APIs)]
Who Can Cannot Argo CD user See Terraform objects of Applications they can get; run actions they are granted (action/infra.argocd.io/Terraform/<action>) Read Secret data (Argo CD redacts it), reach the controller or the runner Controller Read Terraform objects cluster-wide, write their status; read Secrets/ConfigMaps in any namespace (source credentials, fileMappings, cliConfigSecretRef); create/delete runner Pods and TLS Secrets; read Argo CD repo Secrets if enabled Execute Terraform, hold cloud identity, write state — it has no provider credentials of its own and never runs the binary Runner Everything tf-runner in its namespace may do: Secrets, ConfigMaps, Leases (state, plans, outputs); plus whatever cloud identity you give it (env, files, workload identity) Anything in other namespaces; reach sources; accept instructions from anyone but the controller (mTLS)

docs.title: Controller hardening
docs.text:
Shipped by default in install.yaml and the chart:

  • Runs as non-root, read-only root filesystem (writable emptyDir on /tmp for Git clones), all capabilities dropped, seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault.
  • Leader election via Leases; metrics served over HTTPS with authentication/authorization (--metrics-secure); a NetworkPolicy that only admits metrics scrapes from namespaces labelled metrics: enabled.
  • Cluster-wide permissions: the CRD; Pods (runner lifecycle); Secrets and ConfigMaps (source credentials, fileMappings, .tfrc, the mTLS certificates it issues); Events; Leases. It is a privileged component — treat its namespace like Argo CD's own. Reading Argo CD's repository credentials additionally requires the optional RoleBinding in the Argo CD namespace (argocd_repo_reader_binding.yaml, argocd.repoCredentials.enabled), which also covers the argocd-ssh-known-hosts-cm ConfigMap.

docs.title: Runner hardening
docs.text:
Each run executes in a fresh Pod that is deleted afterwards (spec.runner.alwaysCleanup, default). The Pod spec generated by the controller sets: UID 65532, non-root, read-only root filesystem, all capabilities dropped, no privilege escalation, RuntimeDefault seccomp, emptyDir for /tmp and /home/runner. The gRPC server requires a client certificate signed by the controller's CA; the CA rotates (--ca-validity-duration, default 7 days).

You can replace the container security context through spec.runner.podTemplate.spec.securityContext, but anything you set replaces the defaults, so keep the restrictive fields. Workload-identity tokens are readable without extra settings because every container runs as UID 65532 (see Runner Pods › Security context).

Admission policies (Pod Security Admission restricted, Kyverno, Gatekeeper) apply to runner Pods like to any other; the defaults pass the restricted profile.

docs.title: Namespace isolation and tenancy
docs.text:
• The runner identity is per namespace: tf-runner plus a RoleBinding to argocd-terraform-controller-runner-role. A namespace without it cannot run Terraform. Teams therefore cannot read each other's state or outputs through the controller.
  • Cloud permissions follow the ServiceAccount (workload identity) or the Secrets in that namespace — scope them per namespace, or per object with spec.runner.serviceAccountName.
  • --no-cross-namespace-refs (default true) blocks dependsOn and cliConfigSecretRef across namespaces; the object reports AccessDenied.
  • Terraform objects are namespaced, so Argo CD AppProjects' destination and resource allow-lists apply as usual (infra.argocd.io/Terraform).

docs.title: Kubernetes RBAC for people
docs.text:
Three ClusterRoles ship with the install; bind them per namespace or cluster-wide:

ClusterRole Grants argocd-terraform-controller-terraform-viewer-role get, list, watch on terraforms and terraforms/status argocd-terraform-controller-terraform-editor-role viewer + create, update, patch, delete argocd-terraform-controller-terraform-admin-role everything on infra.argocd.io

Remember that kubectl access to Secrets in a namespace means access to the state (and any outputs written there); treat Secret get in Terraform namespaces as sensitive.

docs.title: Argo CD RBAC for people
docs.text:
Approving, re-planning, suspending and force-unlocking from the UI are Argo CD resource actions. Grant them explicitly:

p, role:platform, applications, get, */*, allow
p, role:platform, applications, action/infra.argocd.io/Terraform/approve-plan, */*, allow
p, role:platform, applications, action/infra.argocd.io/Terraform/replan, */*, allow
p, role:platform, applications, action/infra.argocd.io/Terraform/suspend, */*, allow
p, role:platform, applications, action/infra.argocd.io/Terraform/resume, */*, allow
p, role:platform, applications, action/infra.argocd.io/Terraform/force-unlock, */*, allow

Users without action/... permissions still see everything the dashboard shows (plans, outputs names, inventory) if they can get the Application. The plan text lives in a ConfigMap precisely so that it is visible; if plans may contain sensitive values, set spec.storeReadablePlan: none (the UI then shows only the summary) and rely on Git-based approval.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
• State (tfstate-*), plans (tfplan-*), outputs and provider credentials are Kubernetes Secrets. Enable encryption at rest and consider an external KMS provider.
  • Argo CD never sees Secret data through its API, so nothing sensitive leaks into the UI or the Argo CD audit log beyond Secret names.
  • For state outside the cluster (s3, gcs, azurerm, Terraform Cloud) the usual backend security applies; the controller adds nothing.
  • Prefer workload identity over stored cloud credentials; where a Secret is unavoidable, use a dedicated least-privilege principal and rotate it (file mappings and env vars are re-read on every run). See Variables and credentials.

docs.title: Supply chain
docs.text:
• Images are built by GitHub Actions from tagged sources and published to quay.io/redhatworkshops/argocd-terraform-controller-{manager,runner} with the release version as tag; install.yaml and the Helm chart of a release pin those tags.
  • The runner image downloads Terraform from releases.hashicorp.com with SHA256 verification and OpenTofu from the official ghcr.io/opentofu image; versions are build arguments (see Terraform vs OpenTofu).
  • Terraform providers are downloaded by init inside the runner at run time from the public registry (or your mirror via a .tfrc from spec.cliConfigSecretRef). Pin provider versions in your configuration and consider provider_installation filesystem/network mirrors for air-gapped clusters.
  • The UI extension is fetched by argocd-extension-installer from the GitHub release with checksum verification (EXTENSION_CHECKSUM_URL).

docs.title: Reporting a vulnerability
docs.text: Please report security issues privately through GitHub security advisories rather than public issues.

docs.title: Default: Kubernetes backend
docs.text:
When spec.backendConfig and spec.cloud are unset, the controller writes a backend_override.tf into the working directory configuring Terraform's native kubernetes backend:

terraform {
  backend "kubernetes" {
    secret_suffix     = "<object name>"
    in_cluster_config = true
    namespace         = "<object namespace>"
    labels            = { }
  }
}

Consequences:

  • State lives gzip-encoded in Secret tfstate-<workspace>-<name> in the object's namespace (status.stateSecretName). Each workspace gets its own Secret.
  • Locking uses the Lease lock-tfstate-<workspace>-<name>; the lock identifier is reported in status.lock.pending when a run cannot acquire it.
  • The runner writes the state with its ServiceAccount (tf-runner), which is why it needs Secrets/Leases permissions in that namespace.
  • The Secret is visible in the Argo CD resource tree (data redacted) because it lives next to the Terraform object, but it is not owned by it: deleting the object keeps the state unless spec.tfstate.deleteOnDestroy is set.

spec.backendConfig tunes the generated block:

backendConfig:
  secretSuffix: shared-network   # -> tfstate-default-shared-network
  inClusterConfig: true
  configPath: ""                 # kubeconfig path inside the runner (external cluster)
  labels:
    team: platform               # added to the state Secret by the backend

Setting DISABLE_TF_K8S_BACKEND=1 on the controller switches the default to backend "local" (only useful for tests).

docs.title: Other backends
docs.text:
Any backend block can be supplied verbatim and is placed inside terraform {}:

spec:
  backendConfig:
    customConfiguration: |
      backend "s3" {
        bucket         = "my-tfstate"
        key            = "network/terraform.tfstate"
        region         = "us-east-1"
        dynamodb_table = "my-tfstate-locks"
      }
  backendConfigsFrom:            # -backend-config key=value pairs from Secrets/ConfigMaps
  - kind: Secret
    name: s3-backend-credentials
    keys: [access_key, secret_key]

Provider/backends credentials can also come from the runner environment (spec.runner.podTemplate.spec.env|envFrom) or workload identity annotations on tf-runner.

spec.backendConfig.disable: true writes no backend block at all (state stays in the runner's working directory and is lost after the run — only for stateless modules).

docs.title: Terraform Cloud / Enterprise
docs.text:
spec:
  cloud:
    organization: my-org
    hostname: app.terraform.io   # optional
    workspaces:
      name: network              # or tags: [network, prod]
  cliConfigSecretRef:            # Secret with a *.tfrc key holding the credentials block
    name: tfc-credentials

spec.cloud disables the Kubernetes backend; state lives in the TFC workspace.

docs.title: Locks
docs.text:
If a run is interrupted the state may stay locked. The controller reports it:

Ready=False  LockHeld  Terraform Locked with Lock Identifier: f2ab685b-…
status.lock.pending: f2ab685b-…

Unlock by setting (or using the Argo CD Force unlock action):

spec:
  tfstate:
    forceUnlock: yes            # requires lockIdentifier to equal status.lock.pending
    lockIdentifier: f2ab685b-…
    # or: forceUnlock: auto     # unlock whatever is pending — only if nothing else uses the state
    lockTimeout: 2m             # how long plan waits for the lock before failing

Reset forceUnlock to no afterwards.

docs.title: Backup and restore (Kubernetes backend)
docs.text:
Back up the state Secret like any other Secret (Velero, etc.) or by hand:

kubectl get secret tfstate-default-<name> -n <ns> -o jsonpath='{.data.tfstate}' | base64 -d | gzip -d > terraform.tfstate

Restore:

gzip -k terraform.tfstate
kubectl create secret generic tfstate-default-<name> -n <ns> --from-file=tfstate=terraform.tfstate.gz \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -

Migrating to another backend: change spec.backendConfig; init runs with -force-copy, so Terraform migrates the state to the new backend on the next run. Take a backup first.

docs.title: Working with the state from the CLI
docs.text:
Sometimes you need terraform state, terraform import or terraform taint by hand. The Kubernetes backend works from a laptop too; the only difference from the runner is in_cluster_config = false, which makes the backend use your kubeconfig.

  1. Suspend the object so the controller does not run concurrently:

    kubectl -n team-a patch tf network --type merge -p '{"spec":{"suspend":true}}'

  2. Point a working copy at the same Secret. Clone the object's source and, in its path, add an override file (do not commit it):

    # backend_override.tf
terraform {
  backend "kubernetes" {
    secret_suffix     = "network"   # spec.backendConfig.secretSuffix, default: object name
    namespace         = "team-a"
    in_cluster_config = false
    # labels          = { … }       # only if spec.backendConfig.labels is set
  }
}

    terraform init                       # or: tofu init — use the same family as status.binary
terraform workspace select default   # only if spec.workspace is set to something else

    Your kubeconfig user needs get/create/update on Secrets and Leases in that namespace; the argocd-terraform-controller-runner-role ClusterRole is a convenient reference. Provider credentials must be in your shell as usual.

  3. Operate:

    terraform state list
terraform state show aws_s3_bucket.logs
terraform import aws_s3_bucket.legacy legacy-bucket-name
terraform state rm aws_instance.old
terraform force-unlock <lock id>

  4. Resume:

    kubectl -n team-a patch tf network --type merge -p '{"spec":{"suspend":false}}'

    The next reconcile plans against the modified state. If you changed the state in a way that the configuration does not reflect, that plan will show it — which is the point.

Warning

There is no local copy: the Secret is the state. Anything you do with the CLI is immediately what the controller sees. Take a backup first (above). And resist terraform destroy from the CLI unless you also delete or change the object — otherwise the controller recreates everything on the next run because the source still declares it. The GitOps way to destroy is spec.destroy: true or deleting the object with destroyResourcesOnDeletion; see Destroy and deletion.

docs.title: Security notes
docs.text:
• Enable encryption at rest for Secrets in the cluster: the state contains every attribute of every resource, including sensitive ones.
  • Restrict who can read Secrets in namespaces hosting Terraform objects; Argo CD users with applications, get see the Secret's existence but not its data.
  • The runner only has permissions in its own namespace. Give it cloud credentials with the least privilege the configuration needs.

docs.title: Plan storage
docs.text: Plans are separate from state: the binary plan is gzip-encoded in Secret(s) tfplan-<workspace>-<name> (chunked into -0, -1, … when larger than 1 MiB), with the plan ID in the savedPlan annotation. spec.storeReadablePlan: human (default) also writes the terraform show text to ConfigMap tfplan-<workspace>-<name>-readable for the UI; json writes the JSON plan to a Secret; none stores only the binary plan. Plan objects are owned by the Terraform object and are deleted with it.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Start with the object itself — almost every failure is explained by its Ready condition and the last Warning event:

kubectl -n <ns> get tf <name> -o wide
kubectl -n <ns> get tf <name> -o jsonpath='{range .status.conditions[*]}{.type}{"\t"}{.status}{"\t"}{.reason}{"\t"}{.message}{"\n"}{end}'
kubectl -n <ns> get events --field-selector involvedObject.kind=Terraform,involvedObject.name=<name> --sort-by=.lastTimestamp

Then, if needed, the two logs:

# Controller: source fetching, runner lifecycle, decisions (why it planned / skipped / waited)
kubectl -n argocd-terraform-controller-system logs deploy/argocd-terraform-controller-controller-manager -c manager --tail=200 | grep <name>

# Runner: Terraform's own output. The Pod exists only while a run is in progress.
kubectl -n <ns> logs <name>-tf-runner

Turn on debug logging with --zap-log-level=debug on the manager when the decision logic is unclear.

docs.title: By Ready reason
docs.text: Reason What it means What to do SourceFetchFailed Git/OCI fetch or ls-remote failed Check the URL and ref; check secretRef keys (username/password, identity+known_hosts); for useArgoCDRepoCredentials confirm --argocd-namespace and the repo-reader RoleBinding; look for the exact error in the event RunnerConnectionFailed Runner Pod did not become Ready within --runner-creation-timeout, or gRPC could not connect kubectl -n <ns> describe pod <name>-tf-runner: ImagePullBackOff, Pending (resources, nodeSelector, PSA rejection), or a NetworkPolicy blocking the controller → runner port 30000 RunnerQuotaExhausted A ResourceQuota refused the runner Pod Raise the quota or set spec.runner.podTemplate.spec.resources so the Pod fits; it retries automatically AccessDenied dependsOn or cliConfigSecretRef points at another namespace Keep references in-namespace, or run the controller with --no-cross-namespace-refs=false DependencyNotReady A dependsOn target is not Ready, not at the same revision, or its outputs Secret is missing Fix the dependency first;
