this object continues automatically TFExecInitFailed init failed Provider download (egress, registry mirror, .tfrc), backend configuration, module sources, Terraform version constraints — read the runner log BackendConfigurationFailed Generated backend block or backendConfigsFrom is invalid Check spec.backendConfig.customConfiguration HCL and the referenced Secret keys VarsGenerationFailed / TemplateGenerationFailed vars/varsFrom/values could not be resolved, or main.tf.tpl failed to render A referenced Secret/ConfigMap key is missing (mark it optional if that's expected); check template syntax SelectWorkspaceFailed Terraform workspace could not be selected/created Backend does not support workspaces, or the state is locked TFExecPlanFailed plan failed Usually provider authentication or configuration errors — the message is Terraform's; see Provider credentials TerraformPlannedWithChanges (Ready=Unknown) A plan is waiting for approval Not an error. Approve it (UI, Git or kubectl), or set approvePlan: auto TFExecApplyFailed / TFExecDestroyFailed apply/destroy failed part-way State is consistent up to the failure. Fix the cause; the next run re-plans. Check for partially created resources LockHeld State is locked (interrupted run, another process) status.lock.pending has the ID. Use the Force unlock action or spec.tfstate.forceUnlock; see State › Locks DriftDetected Infrastructure differs from state In manual mode: review the drift in the event, then Re-plan and approve. In auto mode this is transient while remediating DriftDetectionFailed The refresh-only plan itself failed Same causes as TFExecPlanFailed; often expired credentials OutputsWritingFailed Outputs Secret could not be written writeOutputsToSecret.outputs names an output that does not exist, or a label/annotation is invalid; or tf-runner lacks Secret permissions HealthChecksFailed A healthChecks entry failed The endpoint is not up yet or the template references a missing output; see the event for the rendered address RetryLimitReached (Stalled) spec.remediation.retries exhausted Fix the cause, then change the spec or source (or Re-plan) to restart DeletionBlockedByDependants Object is being deleted but others dependsOn it Delete the dependants first; Argo CD prune order follows the same rule Suspended spec.suspend: true Resume when ready

docs.title: "Nothing happens" after creating the object
docs.text:
• kubectl -n <ns> get tf: is Ready empty? The controller may not be running, or the CRD/RBAC are from a different release: kubectl -n argocd-terraform-controller-system get deploy.
  • Is there a tf-runner ServiceAccount and RoleBinding in the object's namespace? Without it the runner Pod fails to start or cannot write Secrets (forbidden in the runner log). See Installation › Runner identity.
  • spec.suspend: true? dependsOn not Ready?

docs.title: Argo CD shows the object as Suspended
docs.text: That is a plan waiting for approval (manual mode, the default). It is deliberate: Suspended blocks later sync waves until a human approves. The plan ID is in the Ready message, the event and the UI. Approve it, or use approvePlan: auto for environments where that is acceptable. See Plan approval.

docs.title: Approved in the UI, but Argo CD reverted it
docs.text: The Application has automated sync with selfHeal, so Argo CD put spec.approvePlan back to what Git says. Either approve from Git (commit the plan ID), or add the ignoreDifferences for the action-mutated fields shown in Argo CD integration › GitOps considerations.

docs.title: Provider credentials
docs.text:
Error: failed to get shared config profile, No valid credential sources found, ProviderConfigurationError, Unable to locate credentials: the runner Pod has no credentials. It starts with an empty home and no environment. Provide them with envFrom, fileMappings or workload identity — see Variables and credentials. If they used to work and stopped, temporary credentials (session tokens) expired.

With workload identity: check the runner Pod got the injected env vars (kubectl -n <ns> get pod <name>-tf-runner -o yaml | grep -A1 AWS_ while a run is in progress). If the token file is unreadable (permission denied on /var/run/secrets/eks.amazonaws.com/…), an added initContainer without runAsUser: 65532 is the usual cause — all containers must share the UID for the kubelet to make the projected token readable.

docs.title: The runner Pod is Pending or crash-looping
docs.text:
kubectl -n <ns> describe pod <name>-tf-runner:

  • ImagePullBackOff: the runner image (RUNNER_POD_IMAGE or spec.runner.image) is not reachable; private registries need an imagePullSecrets entry on the tf-runner ServiceAccount.
  • Pending with Insufficient cpu/memory: lower spec.runner.podTemplate.spec.resources or add capacity.
  • Rejected by Pod Security Admission or a policy engine: the default security context satisfies the restricted profile; if you overrode podTemplate.spec.securityContext, keep the restrictive fields.
  • Exits immediately with a TLS error: the per-namespace terraform-runner.tls Secret is stale (controller was reinstalled); delete it and re-plan — the controller recreates it.

docs.title: Source archive too large
docs.text: grpc: received message larger than max: the archived source exceeds --runner-grpc-max-message-size (4 MiB). Exclude what Terraform does not need with spec.source.git.ignore (docs, tests, other stacks), point path at a smaller repository, or raise the flag.

docs.title: Plan is huge / plan Secret chunked
docs.text: Plans over 1 MiB are stored in several Secrets (tfplan-…-0, -1, …); this is normal. If the readable ConfigMap is missing, spec.storeReadablePlan is none, or the plan text exceeded ConfigMap limits — the binary plan is still applied.

docs.title: State is locked after a crash
docs.text: See State › Locks. The Force unlock action in Argo CD is only enabled while status.lock.pending is set, and spec.tfstate.forceUnlock: yes requires lockIdentifier to match — this prevents unlocking someone else's run by accident.

docs.title: I need to run terraform state … or terraform import by hand
docs.text: Suspend the object, then point a local Terraform at the same backend — the Kubernetes backend works from a laptop with in_cluster_config = false. Instructions in State › Working with the state from the CLI. Resume afterwards.

docs.title: The object flaps between Degraded and Progressing, re-planning the same resource
docs.text:
Symptom: Ready=False / DriftDetected on every interval, the drift event always lists the same resource to be created (or changed), applying it succeeds, and the next check finds the same drift again.

The configuration writes something to the runner's filesystem. Every run executes in a fresh Pod whose working directory and home are emptyDir volumes that vanish when the Pod is deleted, so any resource whose "real world" is a local file — local_file, local_sensitive_file, a null_resource with a local-exec that writes a file, a tls_private_key saved with local_file — ceases to exist the moment the run ends. Terraform then sees a resource in state that is missing from the world, and reports drift forever.

Example of the pattern (an SSH key pair written next to the configuration):

resource "tls_private_key" "ssh" { algorithm = "ED25519" }

resource "local_sensitive_file" "private_key" {        # drifts on every run
  filename = "${path.root}/${var.name}-key.pem"
  content  = tls_private_key.ssh.private_key_openssh
}

Fix: keep the value in Terraform's state and hand it out as an output instead of a file. Outputs land in the Secret named by spec.writeOutputsToSecret, which is where secrets belong on Kubernetes:

output "private_key" {
  value     = tls_private_key.ssh.private_key_openssh
  sensitive = true
}

kubectl -n team-a get secret <outputs-secret> -o jsonpath='{.data.private_key}' | base64 -d > key.pem

The same applies to anything a laptop workflow leaves on disk: generated kubeconfigs, certificates, rendered templates, downloaded archives. If a file is genuinely needed by a later resource in the same run, that still works — the file exists for the duration of the run — just do not make it a managed resource that must survive between runs. See Drift detection and Outputs.

docs.title: Installing the UI extension fails with containers[0].image: Required value
docs.text:
The Deployment "argocd-server" is invalid: spec.template.spec.containers[0].image: Required value

The server-extension patch merges into the server container by name (- name: argocd-server). The upstream install.yaml names it argocd-server, but the Argo CD Helm chart names it server. When the name does not match, strategic merge appends a new container that has only the volume mount and no image, and the API rejects it. Detect the real name and rewrite the patch:

SERVER_CONTAINER=$(kubectl get deploy argocd-server -n argocd -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].name}')
curl -fsSL ${RELEASE}/argocd-server-extension-patch.yaml \
  | sed "s/- name: argocd-server/- name: ${SERVER_CONTAINER}/" \
  | kubectl patch deployment argocd-server -n argocd --patch-file /dev/stdin

docs.title: Nothing in the Argo CD UI
docs.text:
• No Terraform entry in the sidebar and no tab: the extension is not installed. kubectl -n argocd exec deploy/argocd-server -- ls /tmp/extensions/resources/ must list extension-terraform.js. If it does, hard-refresh the browser — Argo CD caches extensions.js. If it doesn't, check the extension-terraform init container log on argocd-server.
  • Sidebar entry present but empty: the dashboard lists Terraform objects that belong to Applications you can see. Objects applied with raw kubectl are not shown; neither are Applications your Argo CD RBAC hides.
  • Health shows Progressing/Missing for everything: the argocd-cm patch is not applied, or Argo CD has not reloaded it (it does so within a minute, no restart needed). kubectl -n argocd get cm argocd-cm -o yaml | grep infra.argocd.io_Terraform.
  • Action buttons fail with a Lua error: argocd-cm and the extension are from different releases; re-apply both patches from the same release (Installation › Upgrading).

docs.title: Helm or Argo CD prune deletes the object before the controller destroyed anything
docs.text:
Deletion is handled by a finalizer; the object stays until the destroy (with destroyResourcesOnDeletion) finishes. If the controller is gone (uninstalled first), the finalizer never completes and the object hangs in Terminating. Reinstall the controller, or — if the resources are already gone or you accept leaking them — remove the finalizers manually:

kubectl -n <ns> patch tf <name> --type merge -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":null}}'

Uninstall order is covered in Installation › Uninstalling.

docs.title: Collecting a support bundle
docs.text:
When opening an issue, include (with secrets redacted):

kubectl -n <ns> get tf <name> -o yaml
kubectl -n <ns> get events --field-selector involvedObject.name=<name> --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
kubectl -n argocd-terraform-controller-system logs deploy/argocd-terraform-controller-controller-manager -c manager --since=1h
kubectl -n <ns> logs <name>-tf-runner            # if the Pod is still there
kubectl -n argocd-terraform-controller-system get deploy -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}'

docs.title: User Guide
docs.text:
This section is for the people who write Terraform objects and the configurations they point at.

  • Plan approval workflow — manual approval by plan ID, auto, plan-only, when pending plans are discarded, failures and retries.
  • Sources and credentials — Git and OCI sources, credential Secrets, reusing Argo CD repository credentials, what reaches the runner.
  • Variables and credentials — passing variables (-var, -var-file equivalents) and giving the runner cloud provider credentials.
  • Drift detection — how drift is found, what happens in each approval mode, choosing an interval.
  • Outputs — output names and values, the outputs Secret, feeding workloads and other stacks.
  • Dependencies and health checks — ordering stacks with dependsOn, verifying them with healthChecks, how that composes with sync waves.
  • Destroy and deletion — spec.destroy, what deleting the object does, keeping or removing the state.
  • Runner Pods — image, binary, identity, environment, resources, volumes, security context, networking.
  • Examples — complete objects for common situations.
  • Terraform Specification Reference — every spec and status field. The generated CRD schema is also browsable at doc.crds.dev.

A minimal object looks like this; Argo CD syncs it from your repository like any other manifest:

apiVersion: infra.argocd.io/v1alpha1
kind: Terraform
metadata:
  name: network
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  source:
    git:
      url: https://github.com/my-org/infra
      ref:
        branch: main
  path: ./network
  interval: 10m
  approvePlan: ""          # manual: approve in the UI or set the plan ID here
  runner:
    binary: tofu
  writeOutputsToSecret:
    name: network-outputs

docs.title: API reference: infra.argocd.io/v1alpha1 Terraform
docs.text:
Tip

The generated CRD schema, with every field's type, validation and description, is browsable at doc.crds.dev. This page is the annotated summary.

Short names: tf. Namespaced. Printer columns: Ready, Plan (pending plan ID), Status (Ready condition message) and, with -o wide, Applied (last applied revision).

docs.title: Source and schedule
docs.text: Field Type Description source.git object Git source: url, ref (branch, tag, semver, name, commit), secretRef, useArgoCDRepoCredentials, ignore, recurseSubmodules. source.oci object OCI source: url (oci://…), ref (tag, semver, digest), secretRef, provider, insecure. source.interval duration Source poll interval. Defaults to interval. path string Directory with the .tf files, relative to the source root. interval duration Required. Reconcile / drift-detection interval. retryInterval duration Requeue after a failure (default 15s). retryStrategy StaticInterval | ExponentialBackoff Backoff 2^failures × retryInterval, capped by maxRetryInterval (default 24h). remediation.retries int Attempts before Stalled; 0 none, negative unlimited. suspend bool Pause reconciliation. force bool Unconditionally re-plan and apply.

docs.title: Plan and apply
docs.text: Field Type Description approvePlan string "" manual, auto, disable, or a plan ID (prefix match). planOnly bool Never apply. destroy bool Plan a destroy. destroyResourcesOnDeletion bool Destroy when the object is deleted. disableDriftDetection bool Skip the refresh-only plan between changes. workspace string Terraform workspace (default default). targets []string -target addresses. parallelism int Apply parallelism (0 = default). refreshBeforeApply bool -refresh=true on apply. upgradeOnInit bool init -upgrade (default true). storeReadablePlan none | json | human Readable plan copy (default human, in a ConfigMap). enableInventory bool Record applied resources in status.inventory.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Field Type Description vars[] {name, value \| valueFrom} Variables; valueFrom supports secretKeyRef / configMapKeyRef. varsFrom[] {kind, name, varsKeys, optional} All (or selected, key:newName) keys of a Secret/ConfigMap as variables. Later entries win. values JSON Arbitrary object bound to variable values. tfVarsFiles[] []string -var-file paths relative to the source root. fileMappings[] {secretRef{name,key}, location: home \| workspace, path} Files written into the runner. cliConfigSecretRef SecretReference Secret with one *.tfrc key.

docs.title: State
docs.text: Field Type Description backendConfig object disable, secretSuffix, inClusterConfig, configPath, customConfiguration (verbatim backend block), labels. backendConfigsFrom[] {kind, name, keys, optional} -backend-config key=value from Secrets/ConfigMaps. cloud object Terraform Cloud/Enterprise: organization, hostname, token, workspaces{name \| tags}. tfstate object forceUnlock (no/yes/auto), lockIdentifier, lockTimeout, deleteOnDestroy.

docs.title: Outputs, health and dependencies
docs.text: Field Type Description writeOutputsToSecret {name, outputs[], labels, annotations} Outputs Secret; outputs selects/renames (output:key). Non-string outputs are JSON with a <key>__type companion. healthChecks[] {name, type: tcp \| http, address \| url, timeout} Checks after apply; Go templates over output values. dependsOn[] {name, namespace} Terraform objects that must be Ready first; they cannot be deleted while this object exists.

docs.title: Runner
docs.text: Field Type Description runner.binary auto | terraform | tofu Binary to execute (default auto). runner.image string Runner image override. runner.serviceAccountName string Default tf-runner. runner.alwaysCleanup bool Delete the Pod after each run (default true). runner.terminationGracePeriodSeconds int Default 30. runner.podTemplate object metadata{labels, annotations}, spec{env, envFrom, volumes, volumeMounts, initContainers, nodeSelector, affinity, tolerations, hostAliases, priorityClassName, securityContext, resources}.

docs.text: Field Description conditions[] Ready, Reconciling, Stalled, Plan, Apply, Output, HealthCheck, StateLocked. observedGeneration, lastHandledReconcileAt Bookkeeping; the latter mirrors the infra.argocd.io/reconcile annotation. lastAttemptedRevision, lastPlannedRevision, lastAppliedRevision Source revisions (<ref>@sha1:<sha>). lastPlanAt, lastSuccessfulReconcileAt, lastDriftDetectedAt, lastAppliedByDriftDetectionAt Timestamps. plan pending, lastApplied, isDestroyPlan, isDriftDetectionPlan. lock pending, lastApplied lock identifiers. availableOutputs[] Output names of the last run. inventory.entries[] {n, t, id} when enableInventory. reconciliationFailures Consecutive failures. binary Binary and version used, e.g. tofu 1.13.1. stateSecretName Kubernetes backend state Secret, when used. planConfigMapName ConfigMap with the human readable plan.

docs.title: Annotations
docs.text: Annotation Effect infra.argocd.io/reconcile: <value> A new value triggers an immediate reconcile; with an unapproved pending plan it re-plans.

docs.title: Labels on created objects
docs.text: Object Labels / annotations Runner Pod <name>-tf-runner app.kubernetes.io/name=tf-runner, infra.argocd.io/terraform=<ns>, infra.argocd.io/tls-secret-name Plan Secrets/ConfigMaps infra.argocd.io/plan-name, infra.argocd.io/plan-workspace; annotations savedPlan, encoding: gzip, infra.argocd.io/plan-chunk Runner TLS Secret terraform-runner.tls-<unix> infra.argocd.io/runner-tls=true

docs.title: Plan approval workflow
docs.text:
spec.approvePlan selects the mode:

Value Behaviour "" (default) Manual. Every plan with changes waits until spec.approvePlan matches its ID. auto Every plan is applied immediately; drift is remediated automatically. <plan id> Approves that plan (prefix match allowed, e.g. plan-main). disable Drift detection only: plans run but are never stored or applied.

Related switches: spec.planOnly stops after planning regardless of approval, spec.force re-plans and applies unconditionally, spec.destroy plans a destroy, spec.suspend pauses reconciliation.

docs.title: Plan IDs
docs.text:
A plan ID is derived from the source revision: plan-<ref>-<10 hex chars>, e.g. plan-main-0123456789 for main@sha1:0123456789abcdef…. It is shown in:

  • status.plan.pending
  • the Ready condition message: Plan generated: set approvePlan: "plan-main-0123456789" to approve this plan.
  • the TerraformPlanSucceed event
  • the Argo CD UI (Terraform tab and application view)

The same source revision always produces the same ID, so approving from git is deterministic.

docs.title: Manual approval walkthrough
docs.text:
1. The controller plans and stores the binary plan in Secret tfplan-<workspace>-<name> and the readable plan in ConfigMap tfplan-<workspace>-<name>-readable. status.plan.pending is set and the Ready condition is Unknown/TerraformPlannedWithChanges. Argo CD shows the object as Suspended.
  2. Review the plan: in the UI (Terraform tab) or kubectl get cm tfplan-default-<name>-readable -o jsonpath='{.data.tfplan}'.
  3. Approve:
  4. git: commit spec.approvePlan: plan-main-0123456789 (recommended);
  5. UI: Approve plan button (Argo CD resource action);
  6. kubectl: kubectl patch terraform <name> --type merge -p '{"spec":{"approvePlan":"plan-main-0123456789"}}'.
  7. Before applying, the controller plans again and only applies if the plan ID is unchanged — a source or spec change between approval and apply is never applied silently.
  8. After the apply, status.plan.lastApplied holds the ID and the object is Healthy.

docs.title: When pending plans are discarded
docs.text:
The controller clears status.plan.pending and re-plans when:

  • the source revision changes while the plan is unapproved;
  • the object spec changes (generation) while the plan is unapproved;
  • a reconcile is requested (infra.argocd.io/reconcile annotation, the Re-plan action) while the plan is unapproved;
  • spec.planOnly and the revision changes.

docs.title: Approving from a pipeline
docs.text:
Because the plan ID is deterministic for a revision, approval can be automated without giving up the gate — for example, a CI job that runs after a human review of the plan in the Argo CD UI, or a ChatOps command:

PLAN=$(kubectl -n team-a get tf network -o jsonpath='{.status.plan.pending}')
test -n "$PLAN" || { echo "nothing to approve"; exit 0; }
kubectl -n team-a patch tf network --type merge -p "{\"spec\":{\"approvePlan\":\"$PLAN\"}}"

Or, GitOps-style, have the pipeline commit the ID to the manifest in Git and let Argo CD sync it. The prefix match (plan-main) is convenient for "approve whatever main currently plans" in lower environments, but it also approves future plans for that ref — treat it like auto with a delay.

docs.title: Plan-only mode
docs.text: spec.planOnly: true produces and stores plans but never applies, regardless of approvePlan. The object is Healthy with the plan attached, so an Application can show "here is what would change" without blocking anything. Use it for review environments, or as a dry-run before flipping to manual approval.

docs.title: Destroy
docs.text: spec.destroy: true plans a destroy of everything in the state; the same approval rules apply. Deleting an object with spec.destroyResourcesOnDeletion: true does the same during finalization. Both are covered in Destroy and deletion.

docs.title: Failures and retries
docs.text: Failed runs set Ready=False with a reason such as TFExecPlanFailed, TFExecApplyFailed, SourceFetchFailed, LockHeld or DriftDetected, emit a Warning event with the error, and retry after spec.retryInterval (default 15s; spec.retryStrategy: ExponentialBackoff doubles it per failure up to spec.maxRetryInterval). spec.remediation.retries caps the attempts; the object is then Stalled until the spec or source changes.

docs.title: Dependencies and health checks
docs.text: Two features turn a set of Terraform objects into an ordered, verifiable rollout: spec.dependsOn sequences stacks, spec.healthChecks proves that what a stack created actually answers.

docs.title: Dependencies: spec.dependsOn
docs.text:
apiVersion: infra.argocd.io/v1alpha1
kind: Terraform
metadata:
  name: app-cluster
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  dependsOn:
    - name: network                 # same namespace unless namespace: is set
    - name: shared-dns
      namespace: platform           # requires --no-cross-namespace-refs=false on the controller
  # …

Before each run the controller checks every dependency and waits (Ready=Unknown / DependencyNotReady, Argo CD Progressing, retried after spec.retryInterval) until all of them are:

  1. Ready at their current generation — a dependency whose own plan is waiting for approval, or whose last apply failed, blocks its dependants;
  2. at the same revision, when both objects use the same source URL and ref — so a commit that touches two stacks is applied in order rather than the dependant running against the dependency's previous revision;
  3. done writing outputs — if the dependency has writeOutputsToSecret, that Secret must exist.

Nothing is passed implicitly. To consume a dependency's values, read its outputs Secret with varsFrom (see Outputs › In another Terraform object).

docs.title: Deletion protection
docs.text: When A depends on B, the controller adds a finalizer dependency.infra.argocd.io/A to B. Deleting B first leaves it in Terminating with Ready=False / DeletionBlockedByDependants until A is gone, then B's own deletion (and destroy, if configured) proceeds. This makes kubectl delete -f whole-directory/ and Argo CD prune safe regardless of order: dependants are always destroyed before their dependencies.

docs.title: Dependencies vs. sync waves
docs.text:
Both order things; they operate at different levels:

spec.dependsOn Argo CD sync waves Orders Terraform objects among themselves, continuously (every reconcile) Any resources within one Application, once per sync Blocks on Dependency Ready + same revision + outputs present Previous wave Healthy Works across Applications yes (same cluster) no Deletion dependants first, enforced by finalizers reverse wave order during prune

Use dependsOn between stacks, and sync waves between a stack and the Kubernetes workloads that consume it. They compose: a Terraform object in wave 0 that itself dependsOn another object simply stays Progressing — which holds wave 1 — until its dependency is Ready.

docs.title: Example: three-tier rollout
docs.text:
# wave 0: network (no dependencies)
kind: Terraform
metadata: { name: network, annotations: { argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "0" } }
spec:
  writeOutputsToSecret: { name: network-outputs }
---
# wave 0: database, waits for network through dependsOn
kind: Terraform
metadata: { name: database, annotations: { argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "0" } }
spec:
  dependsOn: [{ name: network }]
  varsFrom: [{ kind: Secret, name: network-outputs, varsKeys: [vpc_id, "private_subnets:subnet_ids"] }]
  writeOutputsToSecret: { name: database-outputs, outputs: ["endpoint:DB_HOST", "password:DB_PASSWORD"] }
  healthChecks:
    - name: db
      type: tcp
      address: "{{ .DB_HOST }}:5432"
---
# wave 1: the application, only after both Terraform objects are Healthy
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: api, annotations: { argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "1" } }
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          envFrom: [{ secretRef: { name: database-outputs } }]

docs.title: Health checks: spec.healthChecks
docs.text:
After a successful apply (and after outputs are written) the controller runs each check from inside the controller Pod. All must pass for the object to become Ready; a failure sets Ready=False / HealthChecksFailed (Argo CD Degraded), emits a Warning event with the rendered target, and the run is retried after spec.retryInterval.

spec:
  writeOutputsToSecret:
    name: web-outputs               # required for templates to see outputs
  healthChecks:
    - name: lb
      type: http
      url: "https://{{ .lb_hostname }}/healthz"
      timeout: 30s                  # default 20s
    - name: db
      type: tcp
      address: "{{ .db_host }}:{{ .db_port }}"
Field Notes type: http + url GET; any 2xx/3xx status passes. Follows redirects. No custom headers or TLS options — use a dedicated health endpoint type: tcp + address host:port; passes when the TCP connection succeeds timeout Per check, default 20s templates Go text/template over the outputs Secret keys (post-rename). A missing key is an error (missingkey=error), not an empty string

Health checks run from the controller, so the target must be reachable from the controller's namespace: a public load balancer, a Service in the cluster, or a private endpoint the cluster can route to. Checks are re-run on the next reconcile only if the previous attempt failed; a Healthy object is not re-checked until something changes.

docs.title: When to use them
docs.text:
• Prove that a managed database, load balancer or cluster is actually accepting connections before Argo CD proceeds to the next sync wave.
  • Catch provider "success" that is not really ready yet (DNS propagation, eventual consistency) and keep the object Degraded until it is.

Don't use them as a monitoring system: they run after applies, not continuously. For ongoing checks use your monitoring stack and Drift detection for configuration drift.

docs.title: Destroy and deletion
docs.text: Terraform-managed infrastructure outlives Pods and Deployments by design, so tearing it down is deliberate. There are two triggers — a flag on the object and the deletion of the object — and one knob for what happens to the state.

docs.title: spec.destroy: true — destroy, keep the object
docs.text:
Sets the next plan to a destroy plan (plan -destroy) for everything in the state. The same approval rules apply as for any other plan: in manual mode the object becomes Suspended with the destroy plan's ID, and the UI marks it destroy; approvePlan: auto destroys immediately.

spec:
  destroy: true
  approvePlan: ""        # review the destroy plan, then approve it

After the destroy: status.plan.lastApplied records the destroy plan, status.plan.isDestroyPlan is true, the outputs Secret is not rewritten, and the object stays Healthy with an empty state. Drift detection is skipped while destroy is set. Flip it back to false (or remove it) and the next plan recreates everything — a convenient way to rebuild an environment from scratch or to park an expensive stack over a weekend.

docs.title: Deleting the object
docs.text:
Deletion is handled by a finalizer, so kubectl delete (or an Argo CD prune) returns immediately but the object stays Terminating until the controller is done:

flowchart TD
    del[Object deleted] --> dep{Other objects<br/>dependsOn this one?}
    dep -- yes --> wait[Ready=False DeletionBlockedByDependants<br/>wait, retry]
    wait --> dep
    dep -- no --> dr{destroyResourcesOnDeletion?}
    dr -- true --> plan[Destroy plan + apply<br/>approval rules apply]
    dr -- false --> clean
    plan --> clean[Delete plan Secrets/ConfigMaps<br/>and the outputs Secret]
    clean --> st{tfstate.deleteOnDestroy<br/>and destroyed?}
    st -- yes --> delstate[Delete state Secret + lock Lease]
    st -- no --> keep[Keep state Secret]
    delstate --> fin[Remove finalizer → object gone]
    keep --> fin

docs.title: Default: keep the infrastructure
docs.text: Without destroyResourcesOnDeletion, deleting the object does not touch the infrastructure. Plan and outputs objects are removed; the state Secret is kept so that a new object with the same name (or backendConfig.secretSuffix) adopts the existing resources on its next plan. This is the safe default for production: removing a manifest from Git by mistake does not delete a database.

docs.title: spec.destroyResourcesOnDeletion: true — destroy, then delete
docs.text:
spec:
  destroyResourcesOnDeletion: true
  tfstate:
    deleteOnDestroy: true          # optional: remove the state Secret and lock Lease too

When the object is deleted the controller runs a destroy plan and applies it under the same approval rules. With manual approval the object sits in Terminating showing the destroy plan until someone approves it (UI action, kubectl patch … approvePlan, or Git if the object still exists in Git — which, during a prune, it does not; use approvePlan: auto or the UI for objects that must self-destroy on prune).

deleteOnDestroy only acts after a successful destroy and only with the Kubernetes backend; other backends keep their state wherever it lives.

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text:
• Dependants first. If other objects dependsOn this one, deletion waits for them (DeletionBlockedByDependants). See Dependencies.
  • Argo CD prune deletes resources in reverse sync-wave order, then waits for finalizers. Put Terraform objects in an earlier wave than their consumers so the consumers are gone before the infrastructure is destroyed.
  • Uninstalling the controller before the objects are gone leaves them in Terminating forever (nobody runs the finalizer). Delete the objects first and wait, or remove the finalizers by hand if the resources are already gone — see Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Choosing a policy
docs.text: Environment Suggested settings Production, shared infrastructure destroyResourcesOnDeletion: false (default). Destroy explicitly with spec.destroy: true + manual approval when really intended Per-team or per-PR environments created by an ApplicationSet destroyResourcesOnDeletion: true, approvePlan: auto, tfstate.deleteOnDestroy: true so pruned Applications leave nothing behind Expensive stacks you want to pause keep the object, toggle spec.destroy

docs.title: What a destroy will not do
docs.text:
• It never deletes the Terraform object's namespace, the tf-runner identity or the credentials Secrets you created.
  • It cannot destroy resources that are in the state but no longer exist in the configuration and are protected by prevent_destroy — Terraform refuses, the apply fails with TFExecDestroyFailed, and the object stays Terminating. Remove the lifecycle rule or the resource from state first (State › Working with the state from the CLI).
  • Resources created outside Terraform (manually, by an operator inside the provisioned cluster) are untouched, which can block the destroy of their parents (a VPC with leftover ENIs, a bucket with objects). Clean those up or add force_destroy-style attributes in the configuration.

docs.title: Drift detection
docs.text: Infrastructure changes outside Terraform — a console edit, an autoscaler, a colleague's terraform apply from a laptop. Drift detection finds those changes on a schedule and either reports them or puts them back.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
On every spec.interval, when nothing else changed — same source revision as the last apply, same object generation, no plan pending — the controller runs a refresh-only plan (plan -refresh=true -out tfdrift) in a runner Pod and compares the real infrastructure with the state:

Result Ready condition Argo CD health Event No differences True / NoDrift — "No drift" Healthy — Differences False / DriftDetected with the plan text as message Degraded Warning DriftDetected with the full plan Plan failed (credentials, lock, provider) False / DriftDetectionFailed Degraded Warning DriftDetectionFailed

What happens next depends on spec.approvePlan:

Mode On drift auto (or spec.force) The run continues: a normal plan is produced and applied immediately. The object goes Degraded → Progressing → Healthy within one reconcile. status.lastAppliedByDriftDetectionAt records it manual ("" or a plan ID) The run stops and reports Degraded, then re-checks on the next interval. Drift is a finding, not a failure: status.reconciliationFailures is not incremented and remediation.retries is unaffected. Review the drift in the event or the UI, then trigger Re-plan: the controller produces a real plan for the remediation, which waits for approval like any other change — unless spec.approvePlan still holds this revision's plan ID, in which case it matches and is applied in the same run (see below) disable Detection only — plans are run but never stored or applied. The object alternates between NoDrift and DriftDetected; use it for auditing stacks that are applied elsewhere

Drift detection is skipped when spec.disableDriftDetection: true, when spec.destroy: true, and while a plan is pending — a pending plan already means "the world differs from the desired state".

docs.title: Interval
docs.text:
spec.interval is both the drift-detection period and the source polling period (unless spec.source.interval sets a faster one). Every detection run costs a runner Pod start, a provider init and a refresh of every resource, so pick it per stack:

Stack Suggested interval Network, IAM, shared databases (drift is dangerous) 10m–30m Application infrastructure 1h Expensive-to-refresh stacks (hundreds of resources, rate-limited APIs) 6h–24h, or disableDriftDetection plus an occasional manual re-plan

When drift detection fails (expired credentials are the usual cause, DriftDetectionFailed), spec.retryInterval and spec.retryStrategy govern the retries like for any other failure. Detected drift, by contrast, is re-checked on spec.interval only: checking sooner cannot change the outcome until someone acts on it, and each check costs a runner Pod and provider API calls.

docs.title: Remediating in manual mode
docs.text:
After DriftDetected, press Re-plan in the Argo CD UI (or set the infra.argocd.io/reconcile annotation). Instead of detecting the same drift again, the controller now plans: the resulting plan is the remediation and is stored as status.plan.pending.

  • If spec.approvePlan is empty or holds a different ID, the object becomes Suspended with the plan ID in its message. Review and approve it as usual.
  • If spec.approvePlan still holds the plan ID of the current revision — the normal situation after approving once from Git — the remediation plan gets the same ID (plan IDs are derived from the revision), matches, and is applied in the same run. Re-plan is then a one-click remediation. To review the remediation first, clear spec.approvePlan before pressing Re-plan.

Any change to the source or to the object spec also produces a fresh plan that includes the accumulated drift, so committing a fix remediates drift as a side effect.

docs.title: Drift that never goes away
docs.text:
If the drift event lists the same resource every time and applying it does not make the drift stop, the resource's "real world" is the runner Pod itself. Each run executes in a fresh Pod whose working directory and home are emptyDir volumes, so resources that are local files — local_file, local_sensitive_file, files written by local-exec — disappear when the run ends and are reported missing on the next check, forever.

Keep such values in state and expose them as outputs (which land in the spec.writeOutputsToSecret Secret) instead of writing them to disk; a tls_private_key saved with local_sensitive_file is the classic case. Files only needed during a run are fine. See Troubleshooting for a worked example and Outputs.

docs.title: Outputs drift
docs.text: After a clean "no drift" result the controller also verifies that the outputs Secret (spec.writeOutputsToSecret) still exists and has exactly the expected keys; if it was deleted or keys were removed, it is rewritten from the state without an apply. Edited values are not detected — the Secret is a projection of the state, not a source of truth.

docs.title: Seeing drift
docs.text:
• Argo CD: the Application turns Degraded; the Terraform tab, the Application tab and the sidebar dashboard show the drift plan under the Ready message. The Re-plan button starts remediation (manual mode asks for approval next).

  • kubectl:

    kubectl -n team-a get tf network -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Ready")].message}'
kubectl -n team-a get events --field-selector reason=DriftDetected --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
kubectl -n team-a get tf network -o jsonpath='{.status.lastDriftDetectedAt}'

  • Prometheus: Argo CD's argocd_app_info{health_status="Degraded"} covers it at the Application level; see Metrics.

docs.title: Drift vs. source changes
docs.text: Drift detection only runs when the source revision is unchanged. A new commit always produces a regular plan, which naturally includes any drift that accumulated — there is no separate "drift" step in that case. Likewise a spec change (new variables, a different workspace) triggers a plan, not a drift check.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Self-healing network stack:

spec:
  interval: 15m
  approvePlan: auto

Audit-only on a stack applied by a CI pipeline elsewhere (the state backend is shared, see State):

spec:
  interval: 1h
  approvePlan: disable
  backendConfig:
    customConfiguration: |
      backend "s3" { … }

Manual gate with a loud alarm:

spec:
  interval: 30m
  approvePlan: ""          # drift ⇒ Degraded until a human re-plans and approves

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Complete, realistic objects you can adapt. All of them assume the controller is installed, the namespace has the runner identity, and Argo CD syncs the manifests (see Getting started). Replace repositories, names and ARNs with your own.

docs.title: 1. Kubernetes resources with the kubernetes provider
docs.text:
The getting-started sample: no cloud credentials, state in the cluster, auto approval, destroy on deletion. The runner's ServiceAccount needs RBAC for what the configuration manages (here a Namespace and a ConfigMap).

apiVersion: infra.argocd.io/v1alpha1
kind: Terraform
metadata:
  name: terraform-sample
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  source:
    git:
      url: https://github.com/redhat-developer/argocd-terraform-controller
      ref:
        branch: main
  path: ./examples/kube-namespace
  interval: 10m
  approvePlan: auto
  runner:
    binary: auto
  writeOutputsToSecret:
    name: terraform-sample-outputs
  destroyResourcesOnDeletion: true

docs.title: 2. AWS stack with IRSA, manual approval, drift alerts
docs.text:
Production posture: credentials come from the ServiceAccount's IAM role, plans wait for approval, drift makes the Application Degraded, outputs feed a health check. The Terraform code pins profile = null (or omits it).

apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: tf-runner
  namespace: platform
  annotations:
    eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/argocd-terraform-platform
---
apiVersion: infra.argocd.io/v1alpha1
kind: Terraform
metadata:
  name: network
  namespace: platform
spec:
  source:
    git:
      url: git@github.com:acme/infra.git
      ref:
        tag: network-v1.4.2            # promote by moving the tag
      secretRef:
        name: infra-git-ssh            # identity + known_hosts
  path: ./stacks/network
  interval: 30m
  approvePlan: ""                      # manual
  runner:
    binary: tofu
    podTemplate:
      spec:
        env:
          - name: AWS_REGION
            value: us-east-1
        resources:
          requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 512Mi }
          limits:   { memory: 2Gi }
  vars:
    - name: environment
      value: prod
    - name: cidr
      value: 10.42.0.0/16
  writeOutputsToSecret:
    name: network-outputs
  healthChecks:
    - name: nat
      type: tcp
      address: "{{ .nat_gateway_ip }}:443"

Approve a plan from Git by committing approvePlan: plan-network-v1.4.2-… (the ID is in the Ready message), or from the Argo CD UI with the ignoreDifferences shown in Argo CD integration.

docs.title: 3. Two stacks in order, outputs flowing between them
docs.text:
The database stack waits for the network stack, reads its outputs, and exposes its own to a workload in the next sync wave.

apiVersion: infra.argocd.io/v1alpha1
kind: Terraform
metadata:
  name: database
  namespace: platform
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "0"
spec:
  source:
    git:
      url: git@github.com:acme/infra.git
      ref: { branch: main }
      secretRef: { name: infra-git-ssh }
  path: ./stacks/database
  interval: 1h
  approvePlan: auto
  dependsOn:
    - name: network
  varsFrom:
    - kind: Secret
      name: network-outputs
      varsKeys:
        - vpc_id
        - private_subnet_ids:subnet_ids_json    # list output arrives as JSON text
  vars:
    - name: db_password
      valueFrom:
        secretKeyRef: { name: database-master, key: password }
  writeOutputsToSecret:
    name: database-outputs
    outputs:
      - endpoint:DB_HOST
      - port:DB_PORT
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
  namespace: platform
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "1"
spec:
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: api } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: api } }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: ghcr.io/acme/api:1.8.0
          envFrom:
            - secretRef: { name: database-outputs }
            - secretRef: { name: database-master }

In stacks/database:

variable "subnet_ids_json" { type = string }
locals { subnet_ids = jsondecode(var.subnet_ids_json) }

docs.title: 4. Existing S3 state, drift detection only
docs.text:
A stack that a CI pipeline applies today. The controller watches it and turns the Application Degraded on drift, without ever applying.

apiVersion: infra.argocd.io/v1alpha1
kind: Terraform
metadata:
  name: legacy-dns
  namespace: platform
spec:
  source:
    git:
      url: https://github.com/acme/legacy-infra.git
      ref: { branch: main }
      useArgoCDRepoCredentials: true   # reuse the credentials Argo CD already has
  path: ./dns
  interval: 1h
  approvePlan: disable
  backendConfig:
    customConfiguration: |
      backend "s3" {
        bucket         = "acme-tfstate"
        key            = "dns/terraform.tfstate"
        region         = "us-east-1"
        dynamodb_table = "acme-tfstate-locks"
      }
  runner:
    podTemplate:
      spec:
        envFrom:
          - secretRef: { name: aws-readonly }    # read-only credentials are enough

docs.title: 5. Per-pull-request environments from an ApplicationSet
docs.text:
Each PR gets a namespace, a Terraform object with auto approval, and everything is destroyed — state included — when the PR closes and Argo CD prunes the Application.

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: ApplicationSet
metadata:
  name: preview-envs
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  generators:
    - pullRequest:
        github: { owner: acme, repo: shop, labels: [preview] }
  template:
    metadata:
      name: "preview-{{number}}"
    spec:
      project: previews
      source:
        repoURL: https://github.com/acme/shop.git
        targetRevision: "{{head_sha}}"
        path: deploy/preview
        helm:
          parameters:
            - name: pr
              value: "{{number}}"
      destination:
        server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
        namespace: "preview-{{number}}"
      syncPolicy:
        automated: { prune: true, selfHeal: true }
        syncOptions: [CreateNamespace=true]

deploy/preview renders the runner identity (ServiceAccount + RoleBinding to argocd-terraform-controller-runner-role) and:

apiVersion: infra.argocd.io/v1alpha1
kind: Terraform
metadata:
  name: preview-{{ .Values.pr }}
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "0"
spec:
  source:
    git:
      url: https://github.com/acme/shop.git
      ref: { branch: main }
      useArgoCDRepoCredentials: true
  path: ./infra/preview
  interval: 1h
  approvePlan: auto
  vars:
    - name: pr_number
      value: {{ .Values.pr }}
  writeOutputsToSecret:
    name: preview-outputs
  destroyResourcesOnDeletion: true
  tfstate:
    deleteOnDestroy: true
  runner:
    podTemplate:
      spec:
        envFrom:
          - secretRef: { name: preview-cloud-creds }

docs.title: 6. Terraform Cloud workspace
docs.text:
State and runs stay in TFC; the controller orchestrates and reports.

apiVersion: infra.argocd.io/v1alpha1
kind: Terraform
metadata:
  name: billing
  namespace: finance
spec:
  source:
    oci:
      url: oci://ghcr.io/acme/tf-billing     # configuration shipped as an OCI artifact
      ref: { semver: "^2.0" }
      secretRef: { name: ghcr-pull }
  interval: 2h
  approvePlan: ""
  cloud:
    organization: acme
    workspaces: { name: billing-prod }
  cliConfigSecretRef:
    name: tfc-credentials                     # key *.tfrc with the credentials block
  runner:
    binary: terraform                         # TFC requires Terraform

docs.title: 7. Kubernetes provider against another cluster
docs.text:
A kubeconfig for the target cluster is mounted from a Secret with fileMappings; the configuration's provider reads it from the runner home.

apiVersion: infra.argocd.io/v1alpha1
kind: Terraform
metadata:
  name: edge-cluster-addons
  namespace: platform
spec:
  source:
    git:
      url: https://github.com/acme/infra.git
      ref: { branch: main }
      useArgoCDRepoCredentials: true
  path: ./clusters/edge/addons
  interval: 30m
  approvePlan: auto
  fileMappings:
    - secretRef: { name: edge-kubeconfig, key: kubeconfig }
      location: home
      path: .kube/config              # provider "kubernetes" { config_path = "~/.kube/config" }

More on each knob: Variables and credentials, Sources, Plan approval, Outputs, Dependencies and health checks, Destroy and deletion, Runner Pods, State.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text: Terraform outputs are how a stack hands values to whatever comes next: a database endpoint to a Deployment, a VPC ID to another stack, a URL to a health check. The controller records output names on the object and, when asked, writes the values to a Secret.

docs.title: Names: status.availableOutputs
docs.text:
After every successful plan/apply the sorted list of output names is stored in status.availableOutputs and shown in the UI (Terraform tab, dashboard). Only names — values never appear in the object or in Argo CD.

kubectl -n team-a get tf network -o jsonpath='{.status.availableOutputs}{"\n"}'

docs.title: Values: spec.writeOutputsToSecret
docs.text:
spec:
  writeOutputsToSecret:
    name: network-outputs           # Secret in the object's namespace
    outputs:                        # optional: select and/or rename
      - vpc_id
      - db_endpoint:DB_HOST         # output "db_endpoint" stored under key "DB_HOST"
    labels:
      team: platform
    annotations:
      reloader.stakater.com/match: "true"
  • Without outputs, all outputs are written, keyed by output name.
  • With outputs, only the listed ones, optionally renamed with output:key — useful to produce UPPER_CASE keys for envFrom.
  • The Secret is owned by the Terraform object: it appears in the Argo CD resource tree, is deleted with the object, and is recreated if removed (see Drift detection › Outputs drift).
  • Sensitive outputs are written like any other — the Secret is the boundary.

docs.title: Value encoding
docs.text:
Output type Secret key Stored as string <key> the raw string anything else (number, bool, list, map, object, …) <key> and <key>__type JSON value, plus the cty type description so consumers can decode it

Example for output "subnets" { value = ["subnet-a", "subnet-b"] }:

kubectl -n team-a get secret network-outputs -o jsonpath='{.data.subnets}' | base64 -d
# ["subnet-a","subnet-b"]
kubectl -n team-a get secret network-outputs -o jsonpath='{.data.subnets__type}' | base64 -d
# ["list","string"]

A string output never gets a __type key, so envFrom consumers only see the keys they expect. Convert non-string outputs to strings in Terraform (jsonencode(...), join(",", ...)) when a plain value is needed.

docs.title: Reading values
docs.text:
# all keys, decoded
kubectl -n team-a get secret network-outputs \
  -o go-template='{{range $k,$v := .data}}{{$k}}={{$v | base64decode}}{{"\n"}}{{end}}'

# one value
kubectl -n team-a get secret network-outputs -o jsonpath='{.data.db_endpoint}' | base64 -d; echo

Or, with the backend override described in State › Working with the state from the CLI: terraform output -json.

docs.title: In a workload, through sync waves
docs.text:
Because an unapproved plan makes the Terraform object Suspended and a failed one Degraded, Argo CD sync waves let a Deployment wait for the infrastructure it needs:

apiVersion: infra.argocd.io/v1alpha1
kind: Terraform
metadata:
  name: database
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "0"
spec:
  # …
  writeOutputsToSecret:
    name: database-outputs
    outputs:
      - endpoint:DB_HOST
      - port:DB_PORT
      - username:DB_USER
      - password:DB_PASSWORD
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "1"
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          envFrom:
            - secretRef:
                name: database-outputs

Argo CD creates the Deployment only after the Terraform object is Healthy — i.e. after the apply wrote database-outputs. If the outputs change later (a new endpoint after a replacement), a Secret reloader such as Reloader restarts the consumers; the controller does not.

docs.title: In another Terraform object
docs.text:
Use spec.dependsOn to order the stacks and spec.varsFrom to read the Secret:

apiVersion: infra.argocd.io/v1alpha1
kind: Terraform
metadata:
  name: app-cluster
spec:
  dependsOn:
    - name: network                # must be Ready, and its outputs Secret must exist
  varsFrom:
    - kind: Secret
      name: network-outputs        # every key becomes a variable: vpc_id, subnets, …
      varsKeys:
        - vpc_id
        - subnets                  # arrives as the JSON text '["subnet-a","subnet-b"]'
  # …

varsFrom passes every Secret/ConfigMap value to Terraform as a string. String outputs therefore round-trip unchanged; non-string outputs arrive as their JSON text, so decode them in the consuming configuration:

variable "subnets" { type = string }
locals { subnets = jsondecode(var.subnets) }

(Alternatively keep complex values as strings on the producing side with jsonencode, which makes the intent explicit in both stacks.) See Dependencies and health checks for the ordering rules.

docs.title: In health checks
docs.text: spec.healthChecks templates can reference outputs by name — {{ .url }}, {{ .host }}:{{ .port }} — when writeOutputsToSecret is set. See Dependencies and health checks.

docs.title: Failure modes
docs.text: Symptom Cause OutputsWritingFailed: "output X not found" outputs lists a name the configuration does not declare (check status.availableOutputs) OutputsWritingFailed: invalid label labels/annotations values must be valid Kubernetes label values Secret exists but is empty The configuration has no outputs, or spec.destroy: true (outputs are not written on destroy) Secret keeps reappearing after deletion Expected — it is owned and reconciled; remove writeOutputsToSecret instead

docs.title: Runner Pods
docs.text:
Every run of a Terraform object happens in a dedicated Pod, <name>-tf-runner, in the object's namespace. spec.runner controls what that Pod looks like.

spec:
  runner:
    binary: auto                     # auto | terraform | tofu
    image: ""                        # override the controller's default runner image
    serviceAccountName: tf-runner    # identity in the namespace (RBAC, workload identity)
    alwaysCleanup: true              # delete the Pod after each run
    terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
    podTemplate:
      metadata:
        labels: {}
        annotations: {}
      spec:
        env: []
        envFrom: []
        volumes: []
        volumeMounts: []
        initContainers: []
        nodeSelector: {}
        affinity: {}
        tolerations: []
        hostAliases: []
        priorityClassName: ""
        securityContext: {}          # replaces the hardened default when set
        resources: {}

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
1. The controller creates the Pod when a run starts (RunnerConnectionFailed after --runner-creation-timeout if it does not become Ready).
  2. The source archive is uploaded over gRPC/mTLS; Terraform runs in /tmp/<namespace>-<name>/<path>; plans, state and outputs are written to the Kubernetes API with the Pod's ServiceAccount.
  3. With alwaysCleanup: true (default) the Pod is deleted when the run ends, successfully or not. The next run starts a fresh Pod.

Important

The Pod's filesystem is ephemeral: the working directory and /home/runner are emptyDir volumes that disappear with the Pod. Anything the configuration writes to disk as a managed resource (local_file, local_sensitive_file, files from local-exec) will be missing on the next run and reported as drift every time. Hand such values out as outputs instead; see Drift that never goes away.

With alwaysCleanup: false the Pod stays between runs and is reused, which saves the image pull and provider download on each reconcile (providers are cached in TF_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR=/tmp/plugin-cache inside the Pod). The controller still replaces it when the TLS certificate rotates or when the Pod has exited; a change to spec.runner (image, env, resources) only takes effect on the next fresh Pod — delete the Pod by hand to force it. Prefer the default unless reconcile latency matters more than the Pod's footprint; a long-lived Pod also keeps credentials in memory longer.

Pods carry labels app.kubernetes.io/name=tf-runner, app.kubernetes.io/instance=tf-runner-<revision>, infra.argocd.io/terraform=<namespace>, plus whatever podTemplate.metadata.labels adds — handy for NetworkPolicies and cost allocation.

docs.title: Image and binary
docs.text:
The default image comes from the controller (RUNNER_POD_IMAGE, pinned per release) and contains both terraform and tofu. binary picks one per object; auto prefers tofu. status.binary records what ran.

Use image for a derived image with extra tools (aws, gcloud, kubectl, sops), pinned provider mirrors, or a single binary — see Terraform vs OpenTofu › Custom runner images. The image must keep the runner entrypoint, UID 65532, and /home/runner + /tmp writable (they are emptyDir mounts).

Private registries: add imagePullSecrets to the tf-runner ServiceAccount (Kubernetes applies them to every Pod using it).

docs.title: Environment
docs.text:
The controller sets POD_NAME, POD_NAMESPACE and forwards its own HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY/NO_PROXY so runners behind the same egress proxy work without configuration. Add your own with env/envFrom: provider credentials, TF_LOG=DEBUG for verbose runner logs, TF_VAR_* (although spec.vars is the preferred way), registry mirrors via TF_CLI_CONFIG_FILE (see spec.cliConfigSecretRef).

spec:
  runner:
    podTemplate:
      spec:
        env:
          - name: TF_LOG
            value: INFO
          - name: AWS_REGION
            value: eu-west-1
        envFrom:
          - secretRef:
              name: aws-creds

docs.title: Resources and scheduling
docs.text:
No requests or limits are set by default. Terraform's footprint is provider-dependent — the AWS and Google providers can use several hundred MiB; large states and -parallelism push it further. Set them explicitly for production stacks, or rely on a namespace LimitRange:

spec:
  runner:
    podTemplate:
      spec:
        resources:
          requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 512Mi }
          limits:   { memory: 2Gi }
        nodeSelector:
          workload: infra
        tolerations:
          - key: infra
            operator: Exists
        priorityClassName: infra-runs

If a ResourceQuota rejects the Pod, the object reports RunnerQuotaExhausted and retries; see Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Volumes and init containers
docs.text:
Mount what the configuration needs — a CA bundle, a kubeconfig for a remote cluster used by the Kubernetes provider, a pre-populated provider mirror — and prepare it with init containers:

spec:
  runner:
    podTemplate:
      spec:
        volumes:
          - name: corp-ca
            configMap: { name: corp-ca-bundle }
          - name: providers
            emptyDir: {}
        volumeMounts:
          - name: corp-ca
            mountPath: /etc/ssl/certs/corp-ca.crt
            subPath: ca.crt
            readOnly: true
          - name: providers
            mountPath: /mirror
        initContainers:
          - name: fetch-providers
            image: registry.example.com/tools/oras:latest
            command: [oras, pull, registry.example.com/tf/providers:2026.10, -o, /mirror]
            volumeMounts: [{ name: providers, mountPath: /mirror }]

For small files from Secrets, spec.fileMappings is simpler than a volume (see Variables and credentials).

docs.title: Security context
docs.text:
The default is hardened: UID 65532, non-root, read-only root filesystem, all capabilities dropped, no privilege escalation, RuntimeDefault seccomp. This is the container security context; setting podTemplate.spec.securityContext replaces the whole block, so restate the restrictive fields when you change one:

spec:
  runner:
    podTemplate:
      spec:
        securityContext:
          runAsNonRoot: true
          runAsUser: 65532
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
          capabilities: { drop: [ALL] }
          seccompProfile: { type: RuntimeDefault }

There is no Pod-level security context (fsGroup, supplementalGroups). Projected ServiceAccount tokens (workload identity) are still readable because the kubelet assigns projected files to the containers' common runAsUser; if you add initContainers, set runAsUser: 65532 on them as well so that rule keeps applying.

Pod Security Admission restricted is satisfied by the defaults; policy engines that mutate Pods (adding sidecars, labels) are fine as long as the runner container itself and the TLS volume are untouched.

docs.title: Networking
docs.text: The controller connects to the runner on port 30000 by Pod IP; the runner needs egress to the Kubernetes API, to provider APIs, to the Terraform registry (or your mirror) and to the source of any remote modules. The runner does not need to reach Git — the controller fetches sources. A NetworkPolicy for a Terraform namespace therefore typically allows: ingress 30000/tcp from the controller namespace, egress to the API server, DNS and 0.0.0.0/0:443 (or your proxy).

docs.title: Sources and credentials
docs.text: The Terraform object carries its own source: the controller fetches it, archives the tree and ships it to the runner. Argo CD only syncs the Terraform object, so the Application repository and the Terraform code repository can differ.

docs.title: Git
docs.text:
spec:
  source:
    git:
      url: https://github.com/my-org/infra.git      # https://, ssh:// or git@host:path
      ref:
        branch: main          # or tag: v1.2.0 | semver: ">=1.0.0 <2.0.0" | commit: <sha> | name: refs/heads/x
      secretRef:
        name: infra-git-credentials
      useArgoCDRepoCredentials: false
      ignore: |               # .gitignore syntax; .git is always excluded
        *.md
        docs/
      recurseSubmodules: false
    interval: 1m              # how often to check for new revisions (default spec.interval)
  path: ./stacks/network      # directory inside the repository

Reference precedence when several are set: commit > name > semver > tag > branch. Revisions are reported as <ref>@sha1:<commit> (e.g. main@sha1:0123…) and drive the plan ID.

docs.title: Credentials Secret
docs.text:
Keys Transport username, password HTTPS basic auth (use a token as password) bearerToken HTTPS bearer token identity, known_hosts (optionally identity.pub) SSH; known_hosts is required unless insecureIgnoreHostKey: "true" ca.crt custom CA for HTTPS 
kubectl create secret generic infra-git-credentials -n team-a \
  --from-literal=username=git --from-literal=password=$GITHUB_TOKEN

docs.title: Reusing Argo CD credentials
docs.text: useArgoCDRepoCredentials: true looks up the Argo CD repository Secret whose url matches (exact repository Secret first, then the longest repo-creds prefix) and the argocd-ssh-known-hosts-cm ConfigMap. Requires the controller to run with --argocd-namespace and to be allowed to read Secrets there (see Argo CD integration). If nothing matches the fetch proceeds anonymously.

docs.title: OCI artifacts
docs.text:
Package the configuration with oras push or any tool producing an image whose first layer is a tar(+gzip) of the tree:

spec:
  source:
    oci:
      url: oci://ghcr.io/my-org/infra
      ref:
        tag: latest            # or semver: "^1.0" | digest: sha256:…
      secretRef:
        name: ghcr-pull        # kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson
      insecure: false
  path: ./network

Revisions are <tag>@sha256:<digest>.

docs.title: What reaches the runner
docs.text:
The archived tree (minus .git and ignore matches) is uploaded over gRPC; --runner-grpc-max-message-size (default 4 MiB) bounds its size. The runner extracts it under /tmp/<namespace>-<name> and works in spec.path.

Additional inputs:

  • spec.vars, spec.varsFrom, spec.values → generated.auto.tfvars.json
  • spec.tfVarsFiles → -var-file (paths relative to the source root)
  • spec.fileMappings → files from Secrets written into the workspace or the runner home (/home/runner), e.g. provider credentials files
  • spec.cliConfigSecretRef → a *.tfrc CLI configuration (TF_CLI_CONFIG_FILE)
  • main.tf.tpl in the path → rendered with the variables (Helm-like {{ .Values.x }}) to main.tf

docs.title: Variables and credentials
docs.text: Terraform runs inside a runner Pod in the Terraform object's namespace, not on your machine. Everything the configuration needs — input variables and provider credentials — has to be declared on the object so the controller can deliver it to that Pod.

docs.title: Input variables
docs.text:
Terraform CLI Terraform object -var foo=bar spec.vars: [{name: foo, value: bar}] -var foo=$(cat secret) spec.vars: [{name: foo, valueFrom: {secretKeyRef: {name: my-secret, key: foo}}}] (or configMapKeyRef) TF_VAR_<key> for every key of a Secret/ConfigMap spec.varsFrom: [{kind: Secret, name: my-secret}], optionally varsKeys: [db_password, "old_key:new_name"] -var-file env/dev.tfvars spec.tfVarsFiles: [env/dev.tfvars] (relative to the source root) -var 'values={...}' spec.values: {…}; the configuration must declare variable "values"

value accepts any JSON type, so complex variables need no HCL quoting:

spec:
  vars:
    - name: instance_count
      value: 3
    - name: enable_logging
      value: true
    - name: tags
      value: { team: platform, env: dev }
    - name: cidrs
      value: ["10.0.0.0/24", "10.0.1.0/24"]
    - name: db_password
      valueFrom:
        secretKeyRef:
          name: db-credentials
          key: password
  varsFrom:
    - kind: ConfigMap
      name: region-settings
    - kind: Secret
      name: api-keys
      varsKeys: ["token:api_token"]   # Secret key "token" becomes variable api_token
      optional: true

spec.values, spec.vars and spec.varsFrom are written to a single generated.auto.tfvars.json in the working directory, in that order, so for the same name varsFrom overrides vars, which overrides values. Terraform loads *.auto.tfvars.json after explicit -var-files, so all of them override spec.tfVarsFiles.

vars[].value and values keep their JSON types (numbers, bools, lists, maps). Everything that comes from a Secret or ConfigMap — vars[].valueFrom and varsFrom — is a string; declare such variables as string and use jsondecode()/tonumber()/tobool() in the configuration when a structured value is encoded in it.

A variable that the configuration does not declare produces Terraform's usual Value for undeclared variable warning in the plan output, not an error — handy for checking the plumbing before the configuration lands.

docs.title: Provider credentials
docs.text: The runner Pod starts with an empty home directory (/home/runner, UID 65532) and no cloud credentials. Pick one of the following; none of them require changes to the Terraform code.

docs.title: Environment variables from a Secret
docs.text:
The conventional Kubernetes way, and what most providers read first (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, GOOGLE_CREDENTIALS, ARM_CLIENT_ID, …):

kubectl -n team-a create secret generic aws-creds \
  --from-literal=AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=… \
  --from-literal=AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=…

spec:
  runner:
    podTemplate:
      spec:
        envFrom:
          - secretRef:
              name: aws-creds
        env:
          - name: AWS_REGION
            value: us-east-1

docs.title: Credentials files (spec.fileMappings)
docs.text:
For providers or configurations that expect a file — an AWS shared credentials file with a named profile, a kubeconfig, a service-account JSON — write a Secret key to a path in the runner before init:

kubectl -n team-a create secret generic aws-credentials \
  --from-file=credentials=$HOME/.aws/credentials

spec:
  fileMappings:
    - secretRef:
        name: aws-credentials      # Secret in the object's namespace
        key: credentials           # key whose value becomes the file content
      location: home               # "home" → /home/runner, "workspace" → the Terraform directory
      path: .aws/credentials       # relative to location → /home/runner/.aws/credentials

Files are rewritten on every run, so updating the Secret and triggering a re-plan is enough to rotate them. Keep in mind that a file copied from a laptop may contain every profile in it, and that temporary credentials (aws_session_token) expire — drift detection on spec.interval will start failing when they do.

docs.title: Workload identity (no stored secret)
docs.text:
On managed clusters, map the runner's ServiceAccount to a cloud identity and let the SDK fetch short-lived credentials itself. The ServiceAccount is tf-runner in the object's namespace, or whatever spec.runner.serviceAccountName says.

  • EKS, IRSA: annotate the ServiceAccount with eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: <role arn>; the role's trust policy allows system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:tf-runner.
  • EKS, Pod Identity: aws eks create-pod-identity-association --namespace <namespace> --service-account tf-runner --role-arn <role arn> ….
  • GKE Workload Identity: annotate with iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account.
  • AKS Workload Identity: annotate with azure.workload.identity/client-id and label the runner Pod with azure.workload.identity/use: "true" through spec.runner.podTemplate.metadata.labels.

The projected ServiceAccount token that these mechanisms inject is readable by the runner as is: the runner container runs with runAsUser: 65532, and the kubelet makes projected-volume files owned by the containers' common UID. Keep it that way if you add initContainers to the runner Pod — give them securityContext.runAsUser: 65532 too, otherwise the token stays root-owned and unreadable. (podTemplate.spec.securityContext is the container security context; there is no Pod-level fsGroup knob.)

Leave any profile argument out of the provider block (or make it nullable, profile = var.aws_profile != "" ? var.aws_profile : null) so the SDK falls through to the injected identity.

docs.title: Kubernetes provider
docs.text: Resources managed with the kubernetes or helm providers in the same cluster need no credentials: the runner's ServiceAccount token is used (in_cluster_config). Grant tf-runner the RBAC for whatever the configuration manages — bind additional (Cluster)Roles in that namespace, or use runner.extraClusterRoles in the Helm chart. The default argocd-terraform-controller-runner-role only covers what the runner itself needs (state, plan and output Secrets, ConfigMaps, Leases).
